articles.title: Meta quer levantar US$ 35 bilhões para financiar seus planos de inteligência artificial | G1
articles.standfirst: Empresa prevê operações que somam US$ 35 bilhões e diz que recursos serão usados para fins corporativos gerais; investimentos incluem IA generativa e desenvolvimento de modelos mais avançados.
articles.summary: Empresa prevê operações que somam US$ 35 bilhões e diz que recursos serão usados para fins corporativos gerais; investimentos incluem IA generativa e desenvolvimento de modelos mais avançados.
articles.body:
Meta quer levantar US$ 35 bilhões para financiar o desenvolvimento de sua inteligência artificial. — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

A Meta planeja levantar US$ 35 bilhões por meio de uma oferta de ações para financiar o desenvolvimento de sua inteligência artificial, segundo documentos divulgados nesta segunda-feira (26) pela Comissão de Valores Mobiliários dos Estados Unidos (SEC).

A empresa controladora do Facebook, Instagram e WhatsApp também anunciou planos para lançar uma oferta adicional de ações de até US$ 60 bilhões, em uma data que ainda será determinada.

Segundo o documento, parte da operação será feita com a emissão de 250 milhões de ações depositárias, ao preço de US$ 50 cada.

Em paralelo, a Meta prevê uma operação de US$ 22,5 bilhões envolvendo ações Classe A. A empresa afirma que não receberá imediatamente os recursos dessa parte da operação.

O documento informa que os recursos líquidos captados serão destinados a “fins corporativos gerais”, sem determinar uma divisão específica dos valores.

No prospecto, porém, a Meta destaca que seus investimentos em inteligência artificial abrangem sistemas de recomendação de conteúdo, ferramentas de publicidade, novos recursos de IA generativa e o desenvolvimento da próxima geração de modelos de inteligência artificial.

A companhia também afirma que trabalha no desenvolvimento da chamada “superinteligência”, definida pela própria Meta como uma inteligência artificial capaz de superar a inteligência humana . Segundo a empresa, ainda é difícil prever quando essa tecnologia poderá ser alcançada, mas os investimentos estão sendo feitos desde já.

Snap elections in Serbia have resulted in the toppling of the long-term leader, Aleksandar Vučić, as protest movement ‘The Student List’ won a decisive victory over the weekend. Over the last two years, students have protested against the government after a concrete roof collapsed outside of a train station and 16 people were killed. articles.title: Thomaz Henrique (PL) contesta eleição e critica vice-governador de SP | G1
articles.standfirst: Thomaz Henrique também voltou a defender maior autonomia para o estado, mas afirmou que a proposta não significa necessariamente defender o separatismo.
articles.summary: Thomaz Henrique (PL) contesta o resultado das eleições, critica o vice-governador Felício Ramuth e defende maior autonomia legislativa para o estado de São Paulo.
articles.body:
De voto no PSOL e leitor de Marx a conservador aliado de Pavanato: quem é Thomaz Henrique, deputado eleito que defende independência de SP — Foto: Reprodução

O deputado estadual eleito Thomaz Henrique (PL) publicou nesta segunda-feira (26) um vídeo nas redes sociais contestando o resultado das eleições presidenciais e dizendo que segue o posicionamento do partido dele.

Sem apresentar qualquer indício de irregularidade, afirmou: “Eu, assim como boa parte do povo brasileiro, tenho dúvidas acerca do processo eleitoral brasileiro”. Na publicação, Thomaz Henrique também disse ter ficado decepcionado com o vice-governador Felício Ramuth (MDB).

Mais cedo nesta segunda, Felício declarou que confia no processo eleitoral brasileiro e questionou a atuação do PL em relação à prorrogação do horário de votação em locais específicos, criticando o fato de possíveis dúvidas terem sido levantadas após a divulgação do resultado.

“O que assombra e me decepciona é que pessoas como o vice-governador Felicio Ramuth, do MDB, após ser recebido em nossa campanha, subido em nosso caminhão de som e pedido voto ao nosso lado, na manhã do dia seguinte ao resultado, vire às costas para o PL e saia nos atacando”, escreveu.

Deputado reafirma defesa de maior autonomia para São Paulo

No vídeo, Thomaz também comenta uma publicação anterior dele em que propõe maior autonomia para o estado de São Paulo. Desta vez, o deputado eleito afirmou que discutir o assunto não significa necessariamente defender a separação de São Paulo do restante do país.

Segundo ele, a proposta seria estudar alternativas jurídicas para ampliar as competências legislativas dos estados e fortalecer a autonomia federativa em relação à União.

“Iniciar uma discussão nesse sentido não se trata necessariamente da defesa de separatismo ou independência, mas sim de elaborar e estudar possibilidades em que propostas de emenda à Constituição permitam ampliar as atribuições e competências legislativas dos Estados”, afirmou.

A Constituição Federal estabelece a organização político-administrativa do Brasil e define as competências da União, dos estados, do Distrito Federal e dos municípios.

O artigo 1º afirma que a República Federativa do Brasil é "formada pela união indissolúvel dos Estados e Municípios e do Distrito Federal". E o artigo 60 trata das emendas à Constituição. O parágrafo quarto afirma que "não será objeto de deliberação a proposta de emenda tendente a abolir: I, a forma federativa do Estado".

articles.title: 60% dos consumidores apontam o bem-estar como motivador na busca por imóveis | G1
articles.standfirst: Tendência mundial impulsiona empreendimentos como o La Vie D’Or, desenvolvido pela Teriva Urbanismo, que integra lazer, natureza e cuidado com a saúde
articles.summary: Tendência mundial impulsiona empreendimentos como o La Vie D’Or, desenvolvido pela Teriva Urbanismo, que integra lazer, natureza e cuidado com a saúde
articles.body:
Imóveis focados em bem-estar e contato com a natureza ganham força — Foto: Perspectiva

A busca pela qualidade de vida tem transformado a maneira como as pessoas escolhem onde morar. Fatores como contato com a natureza, espaços para atividades físicas e ambientes destinados ao descanso ganham relevância na decisão de compra de um imóvel. Nesse cenário, o conceito de wellness real estate, que associa o mercado imobiliário à promoção do bem-estar, vem ampliando sua presença no setor. De acordo com o relatório Wellness Communities and Real Estate Trends for 2026, 60% dos consumidores apontam a saúde e o bem-estar como principais motivadores na busca por imóveis residenciais, um percentual 17% superior ao registrado em 2024.

O dado acompanha uma transformação no comportamento do consumidor, que passa a considerar a moradia também como parte de sua rotina de cuidados pessoais e de qualidade de vida. Segundo o estudo Build Well to Live Well: The Future, publicado pela organização norte-americana Global Wellness Institute (GWI), o mercado de imóveis voltados ao bem-estar registrou crescimento médio anual de 19,5% entre 2019 e 2024, ritmo superior ao da construção civil tradicional, que avançou 5,5% no mesmo período. Acompanhando a cadência de crescimento global, grandes projetos de moradias que valorizam a qualidade de vida também têm surgido em Goiás.

Na região da GO-020, eixo de expansão residencial da Grande Goiânia, o La Vie D’Or reúne características alinhadas ao condomínio-clube, modelo que concentra estruturas de lazer, esporte, convivência e descanso em um mesmo endereço. A ideia é ampliar as possibilidades de uso dos espaços e facilitar o acesso a atividades que contribuem para uma rotina mais equilibrada, sem depender de grandes deslocamentos. O empreendimento residencial de alto padrão conta com 319 lotes residenciais, de 300 m² a 600 m², além de 11 lotes comerciais, com áreas entre 650 m² e 1.000 m².

Condomínio na GO-020 aposta em 'padrão clube' e traz piscina com orla de areia — Foto: Perspectiva

Com projeto arquitetônico assinado pelo escritório Capote Marcondes Longo, do arquiteto Luis Capote, o empreendimento integra a Linha D’Or, que tem como referência o Plateau D’Or, em Goiânia. A proposta combina espaços residenciais amplos, áreas verdes e uma estrutura de lazer conectada a diferentes estilos de vida. Entre os destaques está a piscina com orla de areia integrada ao Bar da Praia, descrita pelas urbanizadoras como inédita na região. De acordo com a Teriva e a Castel, a ideia surgiu como forma de proporcionar uma experiência de lazer que remete ao ambiente praiano em meio ao Centro-Oeste.

Em uma capital cada vez mais acelerada e conectada, torna-se difícil manter momentos verdadeiramente restauradores. Parte disso se deve à falta de contato com o ar livre e com a natureza. Para além do lazer, a ciência tem mostrado que a conexão com o verde influencia diretamente o bem-estar físico e mental. Por exemplo, pesquisas publicadas na revista Ecopsychology demonstraram que apenas dez minutos de exposição diária ao meio ambiente podem proporcionar melhorias significativas no humor e na cognição, além de reduzir a ansiedade e os sintomas depressivos.

Foi pensando nisso que o La Vie D’Or também propõe formas de aproximar os moradores da natureza e conectar os diferentes ambientes do condomínio. A combinação entre lotes amplos, áreas de lazer e serviços de conveniência pretende atender a diferentes necessidades, desde momentos de descanso até atividades em família e encontros sociais. O projeto reúne opções para a prática esportiva, como Lap Pool, Tennis Court, quadra central, quadra poliesportiva, Beach Arena, Green Field e Espaço Calistenia.

Inspirado no conceito de bem-estar, o La Vie D’Or reúne lotes residenciais, complexo esportivo e ambientes integrados à natureza — Foto: Perspectiva

Segundo as urbanizadoras do projeto, a concepção do condomínio surgiu como um novo olhar para a qualidade de vida. “O anseio pelo bem-viver se torna mera consequência em um empreendimento arquitetado para que cada morador possa usufruir do que há de melhor” , afirmaram. A estrutura inclui ainda o Wellness Club, voltado ao cuidado pessoal e ao bem-estar, além de ambientes para convivência e entretenimento, como Grand Salon, Gourmet Grill, Kids Club, Play Lounge, playgrounds, Jardim Pet e Jardim da Mata. O Empório D’Or complementa o projeto ao oferecer uma opção de conveniência dentro do empreendimento.

O La Vie D’Or é resultado da atuação conjunta da Teriva Urbanismo , que reúne mais de dez anos de experiência, e da Castel Urbanismo, empresa com mais de 40 anos de trajetória. Com a expansão do conceito de wellness real estate, mais do que o endereço, a escolha passa a envolver também as experiências possíveis dentro dele e a maneira como os ambientes podem contribuir para melhorar a saúde física, mental e emocional dos moradores.

articles.title: Vitória de Lula no Ceará teve menor abstenção e mobilização nas ruas | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidente reeleito teve 68,39% dos votos no Ceará, estado que registrou a menor abstenção no país e que registrou 480 mil votos a mais para Lula em relação ao 1º turno.
articles.summary: Presidente reeleito teve 68,39% dos votos no Ceará, estado que registrou a menor abstenção no país e que registrou 480 mil votos a mais para Lula em relação ao 1º turno.
articles.body:
A menor abstenção em todo o país , a ocupação das ruas e dos espaços virtuais e a mobilização articulada por jovens lideranças políticas são fatores que ajudam a explicar a vitória expressiva de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) no Ceará no segundo turno das eleições, conforme fontes ouvidas pelo g1 .

No estado, o presidente reeleito conseguiu 68,39% dos votos válidos , contra 31,07% de Flávio Bolsonaro. Lula teve vantagem numérica de votos em todos os municípios do Ceará , incluindo Morrinhos, que foi a única cidade em que Flávio havia vencido no 1º turno . Ao todo, o Ceará teve 480.861 votos a mais para Lula em relação ao 1º turno.

Especialistas ouvidos pelo g1 elencaram aspectos decisivos para estes resultados. Dentre eles, está a redução na abstenção . Nos dois turnos, o Ceará teve os menores índices de pessoas que estavam aptas a votar e que não foram às urnas.

Confira os índices de abstenção no Ceará nas eleições de 2026:

Apoiadores celebram vitória de Lula no bairro Benfica, em Fortaleza — Foto: Thiago Gadelha/SVM

O estado conseguiu diminuir um índice que já era abaixo da média nacional . Para o cientista político Emanuel Freitas, professor da Universidade Estadual do Ceará (Uece), o perfil decisivo para a reeleição de Lula foi o do eleitor que não foi às urnas no 1º turno e que resolveu votar neste domingo (25).

Para o Ceará, o governador Elmano de Freitas (PT) havia anunciado que as metas da campanha eram reduzir a abstenção e aumentar para 70% o percentual de votos em Lula no 2º turno .

O comportamento nas urnas foi parecido com esta projeção, e um dos fatores para esta conquista foi um reflexo da eleição de Elmano como governador e de Cid Gomes (PSB) e Luizianne Lins (Rede) para o Senado, como aponta Emanuel Freitas.

Confira os percentuais de votos no Ceará em 2026:

1º turno: 3.555.263 votos para Lula (63,29%) e 1.756.850 para Flávio (31,27%)

2º turno: 4.036.124 votos para Lula (68,39%) e 1.819.478 para Flávio (31,07%)

“O Lula foi mais votado no Ceará [no 1º turno], o governador do PT foi reeleito e os dois senadores também. Então isso tem um peso simbólico muito forte, porque embora no Legislativo tenha tido um aumento em votação do André [Fernandes, do PL] e dos aliados, por exemplo, mas as disputas majoritárias foram vencidas pela base aliada. Então isso dá um peso muito grande em termos de campanha, em termos de mobilização”, afirma o pesquisador.

Ainda de acordo com o cientista político, outro personagem da política cearense, o senador Camilo Santana (PT), teve um protagonismo nacional ao participar da coordenação de campanha de Lula.

Estes atores, que conseguem articular apoios em cidades do interior, foram elencados como importantes para mobilizar votos para o presidente no Ceará.

Outro aspecto importante para o aumento de votos de Lula no Ceará, principalmente na região metropolitana de Fortaleza , foi a articulação de lideranças mais jovens , como aponta Paula Vieira, cientista política, socióloga e pesquisadora do Laboratório de Estudos sobre Política, Eleições e Mídia, da Universidade Federal do Ceará (UFC).

Dentre os nomes destacados pela pesquisadora, aparecem os do deputado estadual eleito Léo Suricate, do deputado federal eleito Gabriel Biologia e da vereadora de Fortaleza Adriana Gerônimo, todos eles filiados ao PSOL.

De acordo com Paula Vieira, estes jovens adultos têm um perfil de defender as pautas da esquerda de forma mais incisiva, mobilizando as emoções das pessoas nas redes sociais. Na corrida para o 2º turno, estes nomes também levaram estas discussões para as ruas em grandes atos de campanha.

“Eles conseguiram levar para muitos locais da cidade de Fortaleza esse movimento. E eu acho que isso faz a diferença, isso chama a atenção dos jovens, faz com que a campanha seja vista, puxa aí uma leva de jovens que, participando, ouvindo, se sentiram mais instigados a participar do processo eleitoral”, analisa a pesquisadora.

Entre o 1º e o 2º turno, Fortaleza contou também com a visita da deputada federal Erika Hilton (PSOL-SP) em ato no bairro Parangaba.

Para a cientista política, esta presença também teve um impacto positivo entre os eleitores da capital, principalmente pelo protagonismo de Erika Hilton na aprovação do fim da escala 6x1 , sendo esta uma pauta que mobiliza a classe trabalhadora.

Flávio Bolsonaro em ato de campanha em Fortaleza, no mês de setembro — Foto: Thiago Gadelha/SVM

Ainda na análise de Paula Vieira, as duas campanhas buscaram alcançar pessoas que não tinham uma identificação imediata com a esquerda e a ala petista ou com o grupo bolsonarista.

Desta forma, os dois lados buscaram convencer pessoas que tinham escolhido outros candidatos no 1º turno, além dos que votaram em branco e nulo e dos que não foram votar.

No campo de apoio a Flávio Bolsonaro, a capital também teve atos de rua com o ‘Bloquinho do 22’, liderado pelo deputado federal André Fernandes. Na semana anterior à votação, o candidato Flávio Bolsonaro também visitou Fortaleza para participar destes atos.

Para Emanuel Freitas, os atos de campanha por Flávio tiveram menos sucesso em ‘furar a bolha’ e falar com novos eleitores em potencial.

“As duas vezes em que o Flávio veio a Fortaleza, tanto no 1º como no 2º turno, ficaram ali restritas ao Bloco do 22, que é um evento que reúne muita gente, pelo André, pelos deputados famosos, mas que acaba não sendo um momento de promessas, de proposições. Acaba sendo um momento de festa e que acaba falando muito com uma bolha”, analisa o pesquisador.

Ele apontou, também, que uma das dificuldades de adesão do eleitorado cearense à campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro aconteceu por uma falta de propostas e falas que dialogassem com as demandas da região Nordeste.

Neste ponto, Emanuel também recordou que um vídeo publicado pelo deputado federal Nikolas Ferreira (PL-MG) com eleitores do Nordeste reclamando do governo Lula acabou tendo uma reação negativa, mostrando que o apoiador de Flávio desconhece a região.

A mudança no tom da campanha de Lula no Ceará também acompanhou uma tendência observada no Brasil, com o engajamento de estudantes e jovens, a ida da população idosa às ruas, das mobilizações das mulheres e de uma maior presença na comunicação digital.

Para Emanuel Freitas, um dos fenômenos observados nestas eleições foi a "conversão da tia do zap". Segundo ele, este movimento foi o de pessoas idosas antes associadas aos discursos de direita nas redes sociais entrando no "Exército do Lula", do deputado federal André Janones (Rede-MG), que conseguiu encaixar a campanha do presidente na gramática digital.

De acordo com Paula Vieira, uma dinâmica positiva para o campo progressista foi conseguir reconquistar o espaço das ruas e das redes sociais . Segundo a pesquisadora, estes ambientes foram mais dominados por grupos de extrema-direita, desde as manifestações populares de 2013, com movimentos contra o sistema político.

“A partir dali [2013], quem passou a ocupar as ruas não foi mais predominantemente a esquerda. A esquerda mais reagia, ela não pautava as ruas. Em 2018, teve o ‘Ele Não’, então era uma reação à candidatura [de Jair Bolsonaro], e não uma participação propositiva nas ruas. E a esquerda também não dominava as redes sociais”, pontua Paula.

Ainda conforme a pesquisadora, o campo progressista conseguiu mobilizar apoiadores no 2º turno seguindo as orientações de Janones. No Ceará, ela também cita a articulação de Gabriel Biologia e Léo Suricate como figuras que realizaram reuniões com eleitores e orientaram sobre estratégias de comunicação política no ambiente digital.

articles.title: Vaticano confirma viagem do papa Leão XIV a Uruguai, Argentina e Peru | G1
articles.standfirst: Pontífice deve desembarcar na América Latina no dia 6 de novembro e vai passar por Uruguai, Argentina e Peru.
articles.summary: Pontífice deve desembarcar na América Latina no dia 6 de novembro e vai passar por Uruguai, Argentina e Peru.
articles.body:
Papa Leão XIV conduz oração no Vaticano após ter alta do hospital — Foto: Yara Nardi/Reuters

O Vaticano informou nesta segunda-feira (26) que está mantida a viagem do papa Leão XIV ao Uruguai, à Argentina e ao Peru, prevista para ocorrer entre os dias 6 e 17 de novembro.

“Estou feliz por poder voltar ao continente no qual vivi tantos momentos da minha vida", diz o papa em uma comunicação do Vaticano. "Que esta viagem seja uma oportunidade para abrirmos nossos corações uns aos outros, fortalecermos nossa comunhão como irmãos e irmãs e renovarmos nosso compromisso de anunciar o Evangelho com alegria”, continuou.

O comunicado indica que a recuperação do pontífice após uma cirurgia para tratar um câncer de pulmão está evoluindo conforme o esperado e que os médicos o consideraram apto a realizar a viagem.

"Que esta viagem seja uma oportunidade para abrirmos nossos corações uns aos outros, fortalecermos nossa comunhão como irmãos e irmãs e renovarmos nosso compromisso de anunciar o Evangelho com alegria!”, disse o Santo Padre em uma comunicação do Vaticano.

O papa diz aguardar com alegria e entusiasmo a viagem e disse que "oferecerá a oportunidade de fortalecer os laços de comunhão com as Igrejas locais, encorajar os fiéis em sua missão e levar uma mensagem de fé, esperança e paz aos povos do Uruguai, da Argentina e do Peru, encontrar a fé desses povos e partilhar a esperança e a paz que Cristo traz ao nosso mundo”.

articles.title: Storm Boelo: Thousands in Cumbria and North East without power
articles.summary: More than 4,000 homes in Cumbria and north-east England still have no power following Storm Boelo.
articles.body:
Thousands of households across Cumbria and parts of north-eastern England remain without power in the wake of Storm Boelo.

Electricity North West said it was working to restore power supplies to about 3,000 homes, with the worst affected parts of Cumbria including Allerdale, Copeland and South Lakeland.

Additionally Northern Powergrid said hundreds of customers were cut off in Northumberland and County Durham.

On the trains, Northern said disruption was expected on its services between Carlisle and Newcastle, as well as between Lancaster and Barrow.

Derek Story, from Scotby near Carlisle, said it was "disappointing" how long it was taking to get power back on as the lack of a mobile signal meant he felt a bit "isolated".

Stephen Cawley, also from Scotby, said the absence of an internet connection had led his family to spend time together the old-fashioned way.

"We're back to talking to each other and playing Scrabble," he said.

Westmorland and Furness Council said it responded to 90 calls over the weekend, 70 of which involved fallen or dangerous trees.

In Whitehaven, the storm ripped out the power cable running along West Pier.

Whitehaven Harbour Commissioners posted on Facebook: "The pier will remain closed while the cable is recovered from the water and returned to its proper position."

Meanwhile a tree fell on to a completed new-build house at the Homes by Esh development at Havelock Park in Darlington.

It left a huge hole in the roof of the building which was yet to be occupied.

Trees also crashed into allotments near Durham, blocking a footpath leading into the Flass Vale nature reserve.

National Rail said trains between Ashington and Newcastle would not call at Northumberland Park, while services from Newcastle to Ashington would not stop at Blyth Bebside.

Electricity North West offered free welfare support to residents at Cartmel Food Shed Takeaway until 14:00 GMT, as well as at locations in Ulverston and Askam-in-Furness.

Paul Killilea, of Electricity North West, said the majority of homes affected should have their power restored on Monday, but hundreds of homes could remain without power overnight.

"[There is] a significant amount of work to do today," he said.

The A66 reopened on Sunday evening after it was closed in both directions between the A67 near Bowes in County Durham and the A685 near Brough, Cumbria, because of strong winds - a section of road nearly 15 miles long.

The Redheugh Bridge was shut on Sunday afternoon due to high winds but was later reopened.

The Shields Ferry is running following its cancellation on Sunday.

A yellow wind warning was issued in Cumbria, to apply from 18:00 GMT on Monday.

articles.title: An Irish father's 18-carat wedding ring slipped off in an Italian stream; three strangers searched for three days, found it in the riverbed and flew to Ireland to return it to its owner
articles.summary: An Irish father who thought he had lost his wedding ring in a fast-flowing stream in Italy was reunited with it after three local men spent days searching
articles.body: An Irish father who thought he had lost his wedding ring in a fast-flowing stream in Italy was reunited with it after three local men spent days searching the water and then flew to Ireland to return it in person. As reported by American media portal Good News Network, Patrick Mohr was holidaying in Italy with his wife, Joanne McHugh, and their children when the 18-carat gold ring slipped off his finger. The couple had been married for 16 years, making the ring a deeply personal possession.The incident happened while Mohr was playing with his children in the water. One of them grabbed his hand, causing the ring to slide off and disappear downstream. Mohr initially thought it was gone for good. His wife decided to ask the only other people nearby for help. They were three Italian friends: Filippo Palagi, Nicola Malloggi and Edoardo Poggi. Although the men did not have swimming goggles to lend them, they agreed to try to find the ring.Three days of searching the riverAccording to CBC Radio, the three men began their search using kayaks, but their efforts over the first two days proved unsuccessful. They then changed their approach, using snorkelling equipment and securing themselves to boulders with ropes to search a particularly fast-flowing section of the stream. On the third day, Malloggi spotted a glint among the sand on the riverbed. He reached down and retrieved the gold ring.The men later told Mohr about their discovery by sending a photograph to his phone. He was having dinner with his family in Tuscany when the message arrived from an unfamiliar Italian number. The text read: “Hi Sméagol, look what we found.” Sméagol is a character associated with the One Ring in J.R.R. Tolkien’s ‘The Lord of the Rings,’ a reference that reflected the friends’ approach to the search.Speaking to CBC Radio, Mohr recalled his reaction: “I put the phone back in my pocket and kept stirring the pasta pot in shock.” He said his wife noticed his expression and asked what had happened. When he showed the family the message, he recalled, “chaos ensued.” Mohr later reflected on the experience, saying: “Sometimes you have to put things out into the universe and ask for help. And sometimes, you get an answer.”The friends flew to Ireland to return the ringThe three men did not simply post the ring back. They offered to travel to Ireland and hand it over personally, allowing Mohr and his family to continue their holiday without having to arrange an immediate return to Italy. According to Good News Network, Palagi, Malloggi and Poggi took a Ryanair flight to Ireland. Inspired by ‘The Lord of the Rings,’ they arrived at Mohr’s home dressed as hobbits and singing songs from the film series.After the reunion, Mohr took the visitors sightseeing, including a trip to Glendalough in the Wicklow Mountains and the nearby Glenmalure Valley. The group also visited a local pub for Guinness before returning to the family home for a traditional Irish dinner. What began with a lost wedding ring had brought together four men who had been strangers just days earlier. Their search had taken three days, and the journey to return the ring turned the chance meeting into a personal connection between Mohr’s family in Ireland and the three friends in Italy.You use AI every day. articles.title: Nuclear-capable Rafales: Inside France's 'Forward Deterrence' plan to check Russia
articles.summary: Europe is preparing for a future in which the US nuclear umbrella may no longer be taken for granted, and France wants its nuclear-armed Rafale fighter
articles.body: Europe is preparing for a future in which the US nuclear umbrella may no longer be taken for granted, and France wants its nuclear-armed Rafale fighter jets to help keep Russia in check.French President Emmanuel Macron is pushing to extend France's nuclear deterrence across the continent as US President Donald Trump presses European allies to take greater responsibility for their own security, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal.The plan, known as “Forward Deterrence”, could involve deploying nuclear-capable Rafale fighters to allied countries, expanding intelligence sharing and conducting joint military exercises.France would retain sole authority over its nuclear weapons, but the initiative could give European partners a greater role in preparing for a potential confrontation with Moscow.According to The Wall Street Journal, the initiative involves 10 European countries alongside France. The countries involved are United Kingdom, Germany, Poland, the Netherlands, Belgium, Greece, Finland, Norway, Sweden and Denmark.The level of participation varies, with cooperation potentially covering military exercises, intelligence sharing and discussions on nuclear deterrence. Italy has declined to join the initiative, while the three Baltic states Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania — are not part of the current group.The French initiative comes as European governments reconsider how far they can rely on Washington to deter Russia. Trump has repeatedly pressed Nato allies to spend more on defence and take greater responsibility for Europe's security, fuelling debate over the continent's dependence on American military protection.The US remains the backbone of Nato's nuclear deterrence, with American nuclear weapons stationed at several European bases under existing nuclear-sharing arrangements. However, concerns over Washington's future commitments have encouraged France to promote its independent nuclear arsenal as an additional layer of protection.France's approach reflects a longstanding strategic concern that the US might hesitate to risk a nuclear confrontation with Russia to defend a European ally. Paris is seeking to reassure its partners without replacing Nato's existing arrangements or transferring control of its nuclear weapons to other countries.Nuclear-capable Rafale jets at the centre of France's planFrance's Rafale fighter jets could play a key role in the initiative, as the aircraft can carry the country's ASMP-A nuclear-tipped air-launched cruise missile.The missile gives France an airborne nuclear strike capability alongside its submarine-launched nuclear arsenal, allowing Paris to maintain a deterrent that can operate across multiple platforms.Deploying nuclear-capable Rafale fighters to allied countries could expand the locations from which French aircraft operate during a crisis, complicating Russian military planning.The initiative also builds on growing military cooperation between France and its European partners. On October 23, France announced that British Royal Air Force Typhoon fighters had participated in a French airborne nuclear exercise for the first time. The exercise, called Rummy, simulated a nuclear strike mission.

articles.title: As elections near, Iranians fear US and Israel could resume war
articles.summary: Iranians reportedly fear the U.S. and Israel could resume their war against the Islamic regime after the U.S. midterm elections next month and Israel’s election on Tuesday, which could determine Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s political future. The Associated Press reported Monday that residents in Tehran described a growing anxiety within the capital, with some saying…
articles.body:
Iranians reportedly fear the U.S. and Israel could resume their war against the Islamic regime after the U.S. midterm elections next month and Israel’s election on Tuesday, which could determine Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s political future.

The Associated Press reported Monday that residents in Tehran described a growing anxiety within the capital, with some saying they were preparing to leave should strikes resume. Others said Iran’s leadership believes President Trump will authorize new strikes regardless of the outcome of the midterms.

“They’ve accepted that he will attack us again, before or after the elections,” Sasan Karimi, a professor of foreign policy at the University of Tehran and a former government official, told the AP, noting that Iranians were “planning for scenarios so they can take remedial measures.”

Gym trainer Hashem Vajdani told the outlet he plans to leave Tehran.

“I have already packed my belongings to go to a safer town in the north of the country,” he said. “Today I bought more canned food, crackers and extra blankets.”

The greatest concern among those who spoke with the AP was that the civilian death toll could rise if the conflict resumes, particularly after Trump’s threats to destroy Iran’s civilian infrastructure, including its energy grid.

Tehran-based analyst Rahman Ghahremanpour told the AP the results of Israel’s elections could also determine Iran’s future in the near term. The risk if Netanyahu remains in power is that all-out war could commence because of his willingness to take major risks, Ghahremanpour said.

The conflict has remained at a standstill in recent months, with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian accusing the U.S. of disrupting negotiations while Trump regularly threatens the nation with complete annihilation months after the first U.S.-Israeli strikes in February.

Trump and Netanyahu could both face diminished political support after their respective elections, with the Iran war being widely unpopular in the U.S. and a mixed consensus among Israelis on how to confront Iran’s perceived threat, NPR reported .

Middle East Institute senior fellow Natan Sachs told NPR it would be a “shocking surprise” if Netanyahu won another term.

“Israel’s position regarding confrontation with Iran is that it’s not going to be the dove in this conversation,” Sachs said. “So really President Trump is the one who holds the keys here. Israel will be keen to degrade Iran’s capacity and, much more broader than that, the way Netanyahu has put it, to promote regime change in Iran that he still believes can be done or should be done partly through the use of force.”

Trump has warned he could resume strikes on Iran after the midterms. U.S. Central Command has plans ready to conduct follow-up strikes against Iran if there’s authorization from the White House, a source aware of the plans, who spoke on condition of anonymity, previously told The Hill .

articles.title: In Serbia, a very different student movement just ousted another European strongman
articles.summary: Another one of eastern Europe’s authoritarian leaders has been vanquished by an upstart movement, with Serbia’s long-term president Aleksandar Vucic unexpectedly losing out to a student-led campaign.
articles.body: Another one of eastern Europe’s authoritarian leaders has been vanquished by an upstart movement, with Serbia’s long-term president Aleksandar Vucic unexpectedly losing out to a student-led campaign. While young people elsewhere in Europe, especially in France and Italy, have taken to the streets to demand better schooling and opportunities in recent weeks, the Serbian students’ movement had very different origins and goals – and remarkable staying power. It was also a movement more of students in their 20s, rather than their teens – though high school students also became involved. It was also well-disciplined. And despite the government’s efforts to suggest otherwise, it did not include a fringe that sought out confrontation – nor an element more interested in looting. The rise of the Serbian student movement began two years ago in the most unlikely of circumstances. A canopy at a railway station in the northern city of Novi Sad collapsed in November 2024, killing 15 people, including two children. The tragedy, caused by shoddy construction, triggered an outpouring of anger over corruption, the government’s lack of accountability and negligence. Humble origins The protests began with symbolic events. Each Friday the deaths were commemorated with a 15-minute silence, starting at 11:52 a.m. local time, the exact time when the canopy collapsed. When student vigils were harshly dealt with by police, the protests became a campaign. In March last year, more than 300,000 people filled the streets of the capital, Belgrade. In some ways, the student movement emulated US civil rights protests in the 1960s. In January last year, students from Belgrade decided to walk the 100-kilometer (62-mile) distance to join their colleagues from the University of Novi Sad in blocking three city bridges. “By carrying copies of the Constitution with them, the students sought to remind everyone of their fight,” wrote Katarina Beširević of the University of Belgrade, referencing a cycling campaign student demonstrators conducted where they carried copies of country’s Constitution. It was also very inclusive. “A key distinguishing feature of the student movement is its commitment to building civic solidarity across religious, ethnic and regional divides. This includes, for instance, the active inclusion of Muslim and Bosniak students, with respect for their religious identity,” wrote Marta Szpala at the Center for Eastern Studies in Warsaw. Long marches across the country also enabled the students to voice their cause in smaller towns and villages, where people were unaware of the protestors’ aims because of the state’s stranglehold on the media. The movement’s goals soon morphed into something greater. Having begun wanting justice for the victims of Novi Sad, it became about rescuing democracy and civil society from rampant corruption, from elections marked by intimidation and surveillance, and from stifling state control over the media. In that respect it was fundamentally different from student protests elsewhere in Europe. The demonstrations were then institutionalized through the creation of the Students’ List, which scored a stunning victory over Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party at the polls on Sunday. Vucic’s downfall mirrors that of Hungary’s Orban There are strong parallels with Hungary, where strongman Viktor Orbán was defeated earlier this year. Both he and Vucic were in power for more than a decade, were friendly toward Russian President Vladimir Putin, and had gathered immense power through control of the media and corporations. Vucic indeed borrowed from Putin’s playbook, seeking to pivot from president to prime minister when prevented by the Constitution from running again - and playing heavily on Serbian nationalism. Last month, Ratko Mladić, a Bosnian Serb commander convicted of crimes against humanity during the Yugoslav wars, was given a funeral with military honors in Belgrade. There are also parallels between Serbia and Ukraine, where protests by tens of thousands of mainly young people in 2014 ultimately toppled pro-Russian President Viktor Yanukovych amid massive corruption and his refusal to sign an association agreement with the EU. That spontaneous movement feared Ukraine was drifting back into Moscow’s orbit and wanted the country’s identity to be European. It also saw a state that lacked transparency and accountability. Likewise, Serbian protesters asserted their program was “European” in demanding the development of democratic institutions, an independent judiciary, media freedom and the protection of civil liberties. Challenges ahead In Serbia’s case, the evolution of the students’ movement may carry lessons for others. “Volunteers organized into working groups to coordinate logistics, safety, legal aid and digital communications. IT students developed encrypted platforms for secure communication and coordination, while law students and attorneys created a legal-response network to assist detained protesters,” wrote Breza Race Maksimovic and Srdja Popovic in the Journal of Democracy last year. It resulted in a “decentralized yet highly coordinated nature,” they added. “This mobilization is leaderless by design. Student assemblies operate on a horizontal model, organizing nightly plenary meetings to propose, debate, and vote on tactics.” That may have worked well in the face of an authoritarian state; there were no leaders to arrest. But it will be hard to transform into government. And it’s a world apart from the tightly disciplined Hungarian opposition party under Péter Magyar. The challenges ahead for this neophyte movement are daunting. It has few candidates with any experience of governing. The list of candidates for the election was made up of little-known academics, lawyers, athletes, farmers and artists. It will, however,have the support of the European Union. Congratulating the List on its victory, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Monday: “We stand ready to support reforms on the rule of law, media freedom, the fight against corruption and strong democratic institutions.”

articles.title: ‘No oxygen to keep babies warm’: Newborns at risk as fuel shortage hits Yemen’s Taiz amid Houthi-Saudi conflict
articles.summary: A severe fuel shortage in Yemen’s besieged city of Taiz has brought hospitals to the brink of collapse, as weeks of fighting between the country's Houthi
articles.body: A severe fuel shortage in Yemen’s besieged city of Taiz has brought hospitals to the brink of collapse, as weeks of fighting between the country's Houthi rebels and the Saudi-led coalition have disrupted vital supplies and worsened the humanitarian crisis, affecting hundreds of thousands of people.One hospital has been forced to reduce the number of incubators in operation from 40 to just 10, putting the lives of newborn babies at risk.“There’s no oxygen, there’s no fuel to run the incubators, to keep the babies warm,” Reuters quoted Nada Ahmed, a nurse at the Yemeni-Swedish Maternity and Childhood Hospital, as saying.Another staff member, Nawal Najeeb, warned that a “catastrophe” could unfold if fuel supplies fail to arrive.“It will be a catastrophe for the babies, a catastrophe of deaths and disabilities,” Najeeb warned.According to World Health Organization (WHO) spokesperson Christian Lindmeier, 42 health facilities in Taiz are facing severe shortages of fuel, oxygen, medicines and other medical supplies.Fuel prices in the city have also soared to 2,000 Yemeni rials per litre, further straining access to essential resources.Child malnutrition worsensUN agencies and aid organisations have also warned of worsening hunger and malnutrition in Taiz. The World Food Programme (WFP) estimates that more than 800,000 people in the city and its surrounding areas have lost access to food assistance.Unicef spokesperson Ricardo Pires said that, of the 168,000 children screened in Taiz so far this year, 52,000 were found to be acutely malnourished. More than 11,500 of them were suffering from severe acute malnutrition.Unicef has secured nearly 8,000 cartons of life-saving therapeutic food, enough to support treatment services for around three months. However, Pires warned that deteriorating security and movement restrictions could disrupt future deliveries and prevent families from reaching treatment centres.Meanwhile, Doctors Without Borders (MSF) reported that rising displacement was worsening child malnutrition in southern Yemen, a region already grappling with a prolonged hunger crisis. Families have been forced to flee fighting in the north and along the west coast, further straining resources in areas receiving displaced people.Taiz has been largely cut off since October 3, as escalating clashes between the Saudi-backed government and the Iran-aligned Houthis have blocked humanitarian aid from entering the city and prevented civilians from leaving.You use AI every day. articles.title: A 400-year-old Mughal hunting carpet from India passed through the collections of US financier Charles Yerkes, novelist Erich Maria Remarque and the Thyssen family before returning to auction in New York in 2026
articles.summary: Imagine getting your hands on a carpet that was nearly 400 years ago in India! Now this historic Mughal-era carpet is making headlines again.
articles.body: Imagine getting your hands on a carpet that was nearly 400 years ago in India! Now this historic Mughal-era carpet is making headlines again. It’s not just the age but also the design that makes it special. It features hunting scenes, flowering vines and richly coloured motifs. The textile has seen generations and passed through the hands of American financier Charles T. Yerkes, German novelist Erich Maria Remarque and the famous Thyssen-Bornemisza family.More about the historic carpetAlso known as the ‘Yerkes-Remarque’ Mughal hunting carpet, the piece is listed as lot 43 in Sotheby’s Magnum Opus | Evening Auction, held in New York on October 21, 2026. The auction house placed its estimate at 250,000–350,000.A glimpse into the artistry of 17th-century IndiaThe carpet dates to the first half of the 17th century. It is a period linked with the flourishing of courtly art and architecture under the Mughal Empire. The textile measures approximately 473 cm by 200 cm, (15 feet 6 inches by 6 feet 7 inches). The best part about this textile is that it was woven using a wool pile on a cotton foundation.When you first look, its wine-red background offers a perfect setting for flowers, leaves and animals. Then the design goes on to divide into four nearly identical sections. One can see palmettes and rosette blossoms connected by elongated leaves making it more a piece of art. Deep blue, ivory and other vivid shades create contrast adding the perfect colour.The hunting sceneHowever, it’s the hunting scenes that make the carpet compelling. In one section, a tiger appears ready to pounce on a white zebu bull, then you can also see a spotted leopard biting into a blue deer. The border of the carpet features lions attacking or feeding on fawns.Sotheby's 2013 catalogue suggested that the accomplished workmanship points towards a court design workshop. Art historian Friedrich Spuhler also noted that the treatment of the corners indicates the involvement of skilled court designers.The American financier who built a collection to be enviedOne of the earliest documented owners of the carpet was Charles T. Yerkes (1837–1905), an American financier whose business dealings and controversial reputation made him a prominent figure of his time.Yerkes was known for assembling an extraordinary collection of Oriental carpets. According to Sotheby's historical catalogue, the motivation was a personal appreciation of textiles. He wanted to build a collection so exceptional that others would envy it.After Yerkes's death, his collection went under the hammer in 1910. The Mughal hunting carpet was documented in The Yerkes Collection of Oriental Carpets, published in London that year, where it appeared as Plate IX.The sale became an important moment in the history of carpet collecting.Carpet's other famous ownersThe carpet's next famous owner was Erich Maria Remarque (1898–1970), the German novelist best known for All Quiet on the Western Front.The carpet was then associated with Remarque in Ascona, Switzerland, where it remained for several decades. Its ownership history subsequently included a private Swiss collection and The Textile Gallery in London before it entered the Thyssen-Bornemisza Collection in 1986.The Thyssen family connectionHeinrich, Baron Thyssen-Bornemisza (1875–1947), assembled a substantial collection of artworks, including important historical carpets. His son, Hans-Heinrich Thyssen-Bornemisza (1921–2002), later worked to rebuild and expand the family collection.Carpet’s value todayThe carpet's significance lies in the combination of its age, design, craftsmanship and its famous owners. Sotheby's 2013 report recorded repairs and areas of wear. The original pile remained, but the textile showed signs of age and restoration.The carpet had already achieved a notable auction result in 2013.Offered by Sotheby's in London with an estimate of £100,000–£150,000, it sold for £314,500, including the buyer's premium, according to specialist carpet publication HALI.Its return to Sotheby's New York auction calendar in October 2026, with an estimate of 250,000–350,000, brings the story full circle.For a textile created in India centuries ago, the journey of the carpet is extraordinary.You use AI every day. articles.title: Egyptian parliament authorises military aid for Saudi Arabia
articles.summary: Legislators approve military support amid Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, but Cairo has ruled out strikes on Yemen.
articles.body:
Egypt’s parliament has authorised President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to provide military support to Saudi Arabia as attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis intensify.

The House of Representatives, chaired by Speaker Hisham Badawi, approved the mandate in a vote on Monday.

A parliamentary statement members shared with Reuters said el-Sisi had been authorised to “undertake necessary” measures to support Saudi Arabia in defending itself, should Riyadh request assistance.

The move raises the possibility of Egypt becoming more directly involved in a conflict which has consumed the Gulf and the Red Sea in recent weeks.

Nawaf Obaid, a visiting senior research fellow at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera that Saudi officials wanted reassurances that Egypt would support the kingdom if asked.

The vote was Cairo’s way of saying “it will be there”, he said, but questions remain over what type of assistance Riyadh might request and how Egypt would provide it.

The decision follows Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s international airport and facilities belonging to Saudi Arabia’s state oil company, Aramco, which have disrupted flights and oil exports.

The Houthi armed group that controls Yemen’s capital, Sanaa is fighting the Saudi-led coalition which backs the internationally recognised government.

Fighting has intensified in recent weeks, deepening the humanitarian crisis that has already devastated Yemen.

El-Sisi said on Wednesday that any Egyptian military action would be limited to protecting Saudi territory and borders, rather than launching attacks on Yemen.

Egypt’s Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said Cairo continued to favour a diplomatic settlement after visiting Riyadh on Wednesday.

The vote followed closed-door parliamentary discussions and an earlier postponement of the military aid authorisation for Saudi Arabia, which is one of Egypt’s most important economic partners.

Egypt’s constitution requires approval from two-thirds of legislators before troops can be sent abroad on combat missions.

Egypt also has a direct stake in Red Sea security. Houthi attacks near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, the key route to and from the Suez Canal , have disrupted shipping and reduced canal revenue.

Egypt joined a previous Saudi-led campaign in Yemen in 2015, largely helping secure shipping routes with naval forces.

Cairo has not undertaken a large-scale foreign ground deployment since the 1991 Gulf War.

El-Sisi also met United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres in Cairo on Monday to discuss regional tensions and peace efforts.

According to Egypt’s presidency, Guterres praised Cairo’s efforts to prevent escalation in the Gulf and said diplomacy could help address disputes over Iran’s nuclear programme and shipping.

In a post on X on Monday, Guterres urged “maximum restraint”, warning that further fighting could spiral out of control.

articles.title: A San Francisco house valued at about $4.4 million sat empty as its tax debt passed $340,000; after a lawsuit alleged forged ownership deeds, the city approved an auction that could end a yearlong neighborhood dispute
articles.summary: A vacant mansion in San Francisco, valued at about $4.4 million, is set to be sold at a public tax auction.
articles.body: A vacant mansion in San Francisco, valued at about $4.4 million, is set to be sold at a public tax auction. The property has stood empty for years and has built up more than $340,000 in unpaid property taxes. The San Francisco Board of Supervisors unanimously approved a resolution allowing the Treasurer and Tax Collector to sell the Mediterranean-style home at 250 32nd Avenue in the wealthy Sea Cliff neighbourhood. The decision aims to settle a yearlong dispute involving complaints about squatters, police visits and an alleged plan to forge property deeds. The case has drawn the attention of city prosecutors and legal authorities. Because homes worth this much rarely fall so far behind on taxes that the city must force a sale, officials decided to arrange a special tax auction instead of waiting for the usual municipal auction schedule.Unpaid taxes and alleged deed fraudThe property is listed as Assessor’s Block 1391, Lot 014. Wei Wang and her husband bought it in 2013. According to court filings submitted by San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu, Ms Wang later moved abroad and stopped paying property taxes to the city. As a result, the unpaid amount grew to more than $340,000 over several tax years. The long period without anyone living in the house created an opportunity for a series of alleged fraudulent property transfers. In September, City Attorney David Chiu filed a civil lawsuit in San Francisco Superior Court against Brandon Aadee and Diana Peng. He accused them of carrying out "a deliberate and sustained scheme to unlawfully take ownership" of the home by using forged and altered documents. According to the city attorney's complaint, Mr Aadee recorded a fraudulent deed in July 2025. The document falsely claimed that Ms Wang had transferred ownership of the Sea Cliff property to him. Over the next 13 months, Mr Aadee and Ms Peng recorded eight separate deeds, repeatedly transferring the property title between themselves.The lawsuit claims that at least five of these deeds included forged notary signatures, fake seals or official statements that had been changed after notarization. Several licensed notaries told investigators that their signatures and professional seals had been forged or used without permission. Some of the filed deeds also claimed tax exemptions based on an alleged "dissolution of marriage". However, city records show no evidence that Mr Aadee and Ms Peng were ever married. "Defendants are effectively trying to steal a house and sell it to make millions in profit," City Attorney David Chiu said when announcing the lawsuit under California’s Unfair Competition Law. San Francisco Superior Court Judge Charles F. Haines issued a temporary restraining order against Mr Aadee and Ms Peng. The order prevents them from transferring, selling or placing financial claims against the property. It also bars them from filing any more land documents with the Assessor-Recorder's office.Neighborhood frustration and police responseThe legal dispute took place amid growing frustration among residents of Sea Cliff, a quiet neighbourhood near the ocean. According to local news outlet The San Francisco Standard, neighbours had raised concerns for more than a year about unauthorised visitors entering the home at all hours, construction noise outside normal working hours and suspected break-ins. Residents said the empty house had effectively become a gathering place for squatters, leading to frequent calls to law enforcement. The police response also drew criticism from nearby homeowners. Cameron Will, a Sea Cliff resident, filed a formal complaint with the Department of Police Accountability about how officers dealt with an unregistered vehicle parked at the property, according to reports by the SF Inquirer. Another neighbour, Whitney Lynn, said the police presence later improved, with plainclothes officers assigned to carry out targeted checks at the property. District Attorney Brooke Jenkins confirmed that her office had opened an investigation into possible criminal activity linked to the home's occupation and the property title transfers. Speaking to local broadcaster ABC7, District Attorney Jenkins explained that building a fraud case requires strong evidence. She said prosecutors must be sure they can prove criminal intent beyond a reasonable doubt because they "only get one shot at that apple."Public auction to settle tax debtTo recover the unpaid tax revenue and restore stability to the neighbourhood, the San Francisco Board of Supervisors passed File No. 261002. The resolution was introduced through the board's Budget and Finance Committee. It gives Tax Collector José Cisneros the authority to sell the property to the highest bidder at a public tax auction. Under California's revenue and taxation laws, the money raised by the auction will first be used to pay the $340,000 tax debt, along with any accumulated interest, administrative costs and city penalties. Any money left over will be held according to state law. Legitimate lienholders or the verified legal owner may be able to claim the remaining funds. The city has not yet announced an official date for the public auction. However, the Board of Supervisors' unanimous vote clears the way for the tax collector to complete the arrangements and set the sale details.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Saddam Haftar is eyeing the throne in Libya
articles.summary: As the US looks to broker a unity deal, Saddam is trying to position himself as the main contender for the presidency.
articles.body:
Eastern Libya spent nearly seven years denouncing the maritime memorandum Turkiye struck with its rivals based in Tripoli. Last week, it needed a single sitting of the legislature to embrace it.

On October 20, the House of Representatives (HoR) in Benghazi ratified the deal . The European Union condemned the vote, as did Greece, Israel and Egypt.

Yet the ratification was less a Turkish triumph than the final act of a sequence choreographed by Saddam Haftar, the son of Khalifa Haftar, the military commander who controls eastern Libya. The ultimate goal is the Libyan presidency.

The United States is currently trying to broker a power-sharing arrangement between Tripoli and Benghazi. Championed by Massad Boulos, US President Donald Trump’s senior adviser for Arab and African affairs, the deal could install Saddam as Libya’s president.

For that to happen, however, he needs the backing of Ankara, whose sway over western Libya gives it a decisive voice in any such settlement. The ratification of the maritime deal, therefore, is meant to secure Turkiye’s blessing.

The opening move in Saddam’s pursuit of the presidency was a palace coup: a fortnight before the vote, the HoR unseated its speaker, Aguila Saleh , who had spent 12 years in this position. It thus removed both Cairo’s principal ally in the east and the most stubborn obstacle to the memorandum’s ratification.

Yet Saleh’s ouster was never only about Egypt, and the same stone felled a second bird. As speaker and nominal supreme commander, he embodied the de jure authority from which Khalifa’s own command flows, and with a weighty tribal constituency among the Obeidat tribe, he was one of the few men capable of complicating, or even arbitrating, any transfer of power. Removing him cleared Saddam’s path to a handover already quietly under way, which the elder Haftar’s advanced age could hasten at any moment.

Saleh’s successor, Al-Salhin Abdulnabi, a fellow Obeidi, who chaired the HoR’s Libyan-Turkish friendship committee, is able to defuse the risk of tribal backlash while signalling where the chamber now takes its cues.

Whether the gambit pays off will be decided in Washington. Saddam is counting on the Trump administration’s appetite for a Libyan deal, sharpened by Turkish and Emirati lobbying and by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s rapport with Trump.

He hopes it can prevail over the objections of Athens and Nicosia and the displeasure of Israel, which is uneasy about Ankara’s reach. This is directly pitting Trump’s transactional instinct against a longstanding US partnership with the Greek-Cypriot-Israeli axis.

The broadside against Israel may even pay a domestic dividend, allowing Saddam to pose as standing up to Israel while dispelling perceptions of a covert channel to it.

Europe, meanwhile, has sidelined itself into near-irrelevance: when Benghazi expelled the EU’s migration commissioner and three member-state ministers on arrival in July 2025, European capitals responded with something closer to grovelling than resolve.

Less than a year later, Athens was hosting Saddam, who duly sidestepped any commitment on an alternative maritime memorandum.

That deference flows from the EU’s navel-gazing fixation on migration that has reduced its Libya policy to counting the boats leaving Libya’s eastern coast for Crete. A Union that implores Saddam to police the very waters now in dispute is in no position to make him pay for redrawing them.

Abu Dhabi, for its part, has every reason to look the other way because it wants Saddam to succeed. None of Khalifa’s sons has been more faithful to the Emiratis, and seeing their most loyal client installed at the apex of the Libyan state would cap a decade of investment in the Haftar project. Whatever their past flirtation with Greece and Cyprus, a maritime line drawn in Ankara’s favour is a modest price for that outcome, though the closeness of that embrace may yet constrain him.

Egypt remains the real question mark: Cairo’s statement objected chiefly to the memorandum’s encroachment on Egypt’s exclusive economic zone and was framed almost entirely in legal terms, a sign perhaps that it is keeping its political options open.

Its relationship with Ankara has been transformed, with the two now aligned on Sudan and the Red Sea. A shared wariness of Israel’s expansionist ambitions has only drawn them closer.

Offering commercial deals could go some way towards softening Egyptian opposition. But Cairo could also lean on its rapport with Ankara to champion an alternative Haftar heir. It would not have to look far for a candidate: Saddam’s brother Khaled, the Libyan Arab Armed Forces’ chief of staff, is considerably closer to Cairo and publicly criticised the US initiative in April.

Should that happen, Saddam would have little left to bargain with, having cashed in his most valuable chip with the Turks, and the strongest card he still holds is one Abu Dhabi would never let him play.

Cutting off support for Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces would win favour in Ankara and Cairo alike, both backers of the Sudanese army, but that would jeopardise the one relationship he cannot afford to lose.

Squeezed between a patron in Abu Dhabi he dare not cross and a partner in Ankara that has already pocketed its reward, Saddam is betting that he can keep both on side long enough for Washington to see the deal through. That he is prepared to run such risks may say as much about desperation as acumen, for the alternative to an institutionalised succession is one contested, perhaps violently, by his siblings or by the constituencies left out of the new order.

History, in Libya, has a mordant sense of humour. The maritime memorandum was the price Tripoli paid for the Turkish intervention that helped halt Khalifa Haftar’s offensive at the gates of the capital and sent his forces and mercenaries into headlong retreat in 2020. Where the father tried and failed to storm Tripoli, the son now hopes to be ushered in on a red carpet woven from the very document that sealed his father’s defeat.

Should he succeed, the instrument of the Haftars’ most humiliating setback will have become the cornerstone of their dynasty. Should Washington baulk, it may instead become the epitaph of the son’s ambitions.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: World leaders scoff at Trump mulling Orbán as UN secretary-general
articles.summary: World leaders scoffed at President Trump reportedly mulling the idea of nominating his ally former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán as the United Nations secretary-general. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the possibility “funny,” adding “just a moment ago, he was a candidate for president of the European Commission,” according to Politico. He was referring…
articles.body:
World leaders scoffed at President Trump reportedly mulling the idea of nominating his ally former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán as the United Nations secretary-general.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the possibility “funny,” adding “just a moment ago, he was a candidate for president of the European Commission,” according to Politico .

He was referring to a previous claim that Orbán was becoming the European Commission’s president.

Recently, the U.S. has reportedly encouraged Orbán to throw his hat into the ring for secretary-general, according to The Wall Street Journal , citing sources from three countries. A State Department official told the Journal that there were already eight votes on the Security Council for Orbán, while 10 of the 15 council members were within reach.

Ukrainian Foreign Affairs Minister Andrii Sybiha did not seem receptive to the idea on social media , writing, “I am certain that Viktor Orbán, as UN Secretary-General, would put to good use the masterful veto and blackmail skills he has developed over years of derailing major EU decisions.”

“We can share with the rest of the world our great experience of taking him out for coffee at the right moment,” he added.

Orbán has faced criticism for weaponizing the justice system to go after political opponents and critics, failing to meaningfully tackle corruption and undermining freedom of speech, as well as unfair practices in elections.

Shashi Tharoor, a senior leader of the Indian opposition Congress party and former secretary-general candidate, similarly wrote , “what are the odds of @PM_ViktorOrban actually getting the minimum nine votes required from non-permanent members of the @un Security Council? I wouldn’t rate them too highly!”

The appointment process of selecting the next U.N. secretary-general kicked off in 2025 with seven nominees currently listed on the U.N.’s website as top contenders for the role.

Orbán is not listed, and in order to be elected by the General Assembly, the Security Council must provide a recommendation for a candidate.

The candidate must have support from nine of the 15 Security Council members, without opposition from any permanent members — China, France, Russia, U.K. and U.S. — which can block a nominee with veto power. The requirements have made finding the next secretary-general difficult.

Reports about Orbán’s potential nomination are also receiving pushback stateside.

Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) called it a “terrible choice” on social media .

In the past, Trump endorsed Orbán’s reelection bid for Hungarian prime minister and even hosted him at the White House last year. The visit focused on Orbán asking Trump to provide Hungary with an exemption to continue importing Russian oil despite U.S. sanctions.

articles.title: Israelis and Americans are both voting - with global consequences
articles.summary: The next fortnight sees two elections on different continents. The outcomes will shape geopolitics and the global economy, writes James Landale
articles.body:
In the next week, two sets of elections will be held on two continents, the outcomes of which could have profound consequences for the world.

By a fluke of electoral timetabling, millions of voters around 6,000 miles apart will unite in exercising their democratic rights within days of each other.

Voters in Israel go to the polls on Tuesday to elect a new parliament; a week later, voters in the United States will elect a new Congress.

A former speaker of that Congress, Tip O'Neill, may have once said that "all politics is local". But the consequences of these elections will undoubtedly be global.

For these elections are not just proximate, they are intertwined.

The future governance of Israel will have a lasting impact on the Middle East and wars raging across the region.

And any change in the electoral map of America could shape not just those wars but also the future of the global economy.

Between the two there is a physical connection: the lobby group Republicans Overseas Israel estimates about half a million Israelis with American passports can vote in both polls.

Marc Zell, the group's chairman, said these electors could influence tight races in the US, such as the Michigan senatorial contest, in which he estimated 10,000 absentee ballots would be cast from Israel. "They can really make a difference," he told the BBC.

But the policy connection is perhaps deeper - and most acute regarding the US-Israeli war on Iran. The massive aerial attack, which began in February, destroyed many military targets and killed much of Iran's leadership. But it failed to overthrow the regime which hit back hard across the Gulf and seized control of the Strait of Hormuz and the energy that flowed through it.

The sheer fact of the elections has already shaped decision-making.

Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has used the campaign to talk up the possibility of launching a fresh attack on Iran.

He has made new claims – without providing evidence – about Iran's nuclear threat, insisting again the Islamic regime must be overthrown.

His aim: to shore up his reputation as a security leader, which took such a battering after the deadly 7 October Hamas-led attacks on Israel.

US President Donald Trump has added to the speculation of renewed attacks on Iran by endorsing Netanyahu's re-election campaign, saying both men should "soon finish the job" in Iran.

Yet for all the sabre-rattling, there have also been contradictory reports that Trump intervened to restrain Netanyahu from attacking Iran before polling day, fearing a fresh spike in energy prices would remind US voters of his unpopular war.

So might an attack on Iran, then, be delayed until after the elections? Israel's media is full of speculation Netanyahu could try to engineer his survival by attacking Iran as caretaker prime minister after the election.

He would argue, so the theory goes, for a government of national unity – involving him – rather than a coalition between opposition parties. Netanyahu has long been seen as a great survivor of Israeli politics. If he were to lose power, he would face an official inquiry into his actions before the October 7 attacks and renewed legal proceedings involving allegations of corruption.

So real is this speculation that Netanyahu's rival, the former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has already ruled out joining any unity government. Like all mainstream Israeli politicians, Eisenkot sees Iran as an existential threat to Israel and supports military action against the Islamic regime. But he has explicitly warned against escalating the war for political purposes.

Certainly, Trump may be more willing to attack Iran after the midterms if he is unconstrained electorally and hoping to extract himself from the war with one more push. Some analysts believe Iran is so economically weak from the war and economic sanctions that a fresh round of military strikes might encourage Iranians to overthrow the regime. Others see this as yet more wishful thinking. It is a strategy that has repeatedly failed, but still has currency in Washington.

"After the midterms, he will be in legacy mode," one well-placed Western diplomat told me. "He will want to show agency on anything that is not the quagmire at home."

In Israel there is a broad consensus across most parties about the threat from and the need to constrain Iran. But if voters elect a new government, they might have a prime minister with less political and personal investment in fresh attacks.

In those circumstances, Trump has suggested his thinking may change, too. "If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi [a nickname for Netanyahu], America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," he wrote on social media.

Little wonder policymakers in Tehran have been following US opinion polls as closely as any analyst inside the Washington beltway. The risk, of course, is that any post-electoral strikes would plunge the Middle East into fresh chaos if Iran were to retaliate hard.

Publicly and privately, Iranian officials have threatened to hit airports, pipelines, undersea cables, energy facilities, desalination plants as well as US bases and warships.

Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, wrote in the Financial Times that new attacks would put "civilian lives and the wellbeing of all regional states and the global economy at great risk".

The two elections again intertwine around the global economy. Affordability and cost of living have dominated campaigning for the midterms, issues made worse by Trump's war that raised prices as Iran choked the flow of energy through the Strait of Hormuz.

The economy is also an election issue in Israel, where voters face high costs and low wages. But here, too, the war plays its part with soaring defence spending putting even more pressure on the public finances.

Trump has sought to appease voters ahead of the midterms. He has lifted sanctions on Russia, hoping in vain that by importing diesel from Moscow, prices might fall significantly. He has been taking a tough line with Ukraine, calling on its leadership to make concessions in the hope – also so far in vain – of claiming a foreign policy victory.

But Republican ire at his controversial strategy is growing. Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina, a frequent critic of Trump, told CBS News: "If the President wants to actually bring down energy prices, he can do it by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid [favour] for Vladimir Putin."

One consequence of the Iran war – along with Israel's military operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank – is that traditional bipartisan support in the US has fractured. Abdul El-Sayed, the left-wing Democratic candidate for the Senate in Michigan, campaigns on cutting military aid to Israel. "An ally that takes your money, to push you into wars you shouldn't be fighting, is not an ally," he told ABC News.

The US and Israel initially attacked Iran to destroy its ballistic missiles, degrade its nuclear capability, weaken its support for proxy militias and even oust the entire regime. Since then its war aims have changed to reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

Brad Lander, a Democratic congressional candidate in New York who also sits on the left of his party, chose even to travel to the West Bank only days before polling. He helped Palestinians harvest olives and was briefly detained by Israeli forces, all grist to his social media electoral mill. In the history of US politics, this is not normal. Even Netanyahu is warning that Israel may in future have to survive without a US security blanket.

Of course, if Israel's prime minister were to lose, his departure would end a scratchy bromance that has seen Trump blow hot and cold. Last week the president called his Israeli counterpart a "great warrior prime minister". During the summer, he said Netanyahu was "effing crazy". A new Israeli leader would have to forge a new relationship with an outgoing US president, a very different dynamic.

If the Democrats were to win greater control in Congress, that might place some check on blanket US support for Israel. Congress has traditional powers that it can use to restrain military spending. It could also cut military aid to Israel. But as president, Trump would retain significant executive power – and a veto – to continue prosecuting the conflict as he saw fit.

The decision by Israel and the US to go to war with Iran earlier this year transformed the global economy and international geopolitics. The choices voters in both nations make in coming days may shape where the world goes next.

articles.title: Army officer killed by reversing Warrior with faulty alarm - inquest
articles.summary: Second Lt Max George, 26, died during a training exercise on Salisbury Plain, an inquest is told.
articles.body:
An Army officer died when a Warrior armoured vehicle with a broken safety alarm was reversed into him, an inquest has been told.

Second Lt Max George, 26, of Durham, died at the scene of a training exercise on Salisbury Plain, Wiltshire, on 21 June 2022.

The ongoing inquest at Wiltshire and Swindon Coroner's Court heard an alarm, which was designed to alert the driver when the Warrior's rear doors were open, had been faulty since 2018.

Lt Col Graham Watson, who led a service inquiry into the incident, said the driver of the Warrior "would have almost certainly stopped" if the alarm had sounded.

Members of 5 Rifles got up at 05:00 BST on the day of the incident and left their barracks at 07:00, the inquest heard.

They were undertaking an exercise called Combat Spirit, which formed the final part of four courses to qualify for Armoured Infantry.

The inquest heard two groups of soldiers had converged on a target and 2nd Lt George was ordered to leave the Warrior through a rear door and take command on the ground.

"[Second] Lt George exited the vehicle and was seen momentarily struggling either with a day sack or trying to free a radio antenna, which may have snagged," Col Watson said.

"He then went to grab his weapon, which was still inside the vehicle and, simultaneously, the student commander commanded the gunner to reverse."

Second Lt George's exit from the Warrior created a "clunking noise", which may have led the commander to assume he was safely off the vehicle and had shut the doors, Col Watson added.

The armoured vehicle was stationary for between 38 and 43 seconds after the collision, the inquest heard, as soldiers shouted "wait" and horns sounded.

A stop call was sent at 10:25, which halted the exercise.

A built-in alarm system, which would have sounded a noise and shown a light to indicate the rear doors were open, did not work as a wire was broken, the inquest was told.

Col Watson said: "The built-in alarm would have alarmed because the rear doors were open, and had that gone off the driver would have almost certainly stopped."

Alarms had been installed on Warriors after two fatal incidents in the 1990s.

Col Watson said several faults with the armoured vehicles were known about, but he told the inquest that these had not meant the vehicle should have been taken out of service.

The inquest also heard the FV-511model involved in the incident was not ordinarily used for disembarking troops and close combat.

"The student commander had done the majority of his training on the FV-510, which is the platoon variant of the vehicle," Col Watson said.

"In general, the crew and service personnel within 5 Rifles were not that familiar with the FV-511 and its differences with the FV-510."

A pen portrait was read out by 2nd Lt George's mother, Vivienne, during the hearing.

She described her son as "modest and great fun" and said he would "quietly" fundraise through events like the Great North Run and Royal British Legion street collections.

Second Lt George had won the Queen's Medal for best cadet when he passed out from the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst, the inquest was told.

He had also attended Durham School, earned a first in politics with Russian at Newcastle University and obtained a Distinction in his Masters in Eastern European and Eurasian Studies with Russian at the University of Glasgow.

His mother continued: "Max had effortless leadership qualities and his potential was enormous," she said.

"His loss has left a hole in our lives, he was the very best of all of us."
