articles.title: In 2020, a Michigan couple agreed to pay $1.275 million for a home but sought a $150,000 discount after inspection; six years later, an October 23 court overturned a $1.55 million judgment against them
articles.summary: A Michigan appeals court has overturned a $1.55 million judgment against a couple who backed out of buying a luxury home after an inspection revealed
articles.body: A Michigan appeals court has overturned a $1.55 million judgment against a couple who backed out of buying a luxury home after an inspection revealed serious problems with the property. In a ruling published on October 23, 2026, the Michigan Court of Appeals cleared the couple of responsibility for the damages, ending a legal dispute that lasted six years. The appeals court found that the sellers had failed to prove that the buyers broke their contract when they asked for a lower price after the home inspection. According to court documents published by Justia Law, the dispute began in 2020 when the couple agreed to buy the home for $1.275 million. The purchase agreement included standard inspection conditions, which allowed the buyers to check the property's condition before completing the sale. During a professional inspection, inspectors and structural experts found several serious problems with the house. After reviewing the findings, the buyers formally asked for a $150,000 reduction in the agreed price to help cover the expected cost of repairs.Failed negotiations lead to litigationThe sellers refused to lower the price, and negotiations broke down. When the buyers declined to pay the original $1.275 million without repairs or financial compensation, the sellers filed a lawsuit, claiming that the couple had broken the contract. A trial court initially ruled in favour of the sellers. It held the buyers responsible for failing to complete the purchase. The lower court ordered the couple to pay $1.55 million in damages. This amount included the difference in the home's resale value, the costs of holding the property and legal interest that had built up during the years of litigation. The buyers then appealed the decision. They argued that the purchase agreement allowed them to request a lower price or cancel the deal if the home inspection revealed problems that they found unacceptable.Appeals panel sets aside damagesAfter reviewing the lower court's decision, the Michigan Court of Appeals found that the trial judge had misunderstood the contract's inspection terms. The three-judge panel said that asking for a price reduction because of documented defects in the property did not amount to breaking the agreement. The appeals court explained that the buyers had acted within the terms of the contract when they asked for changes based on the home's condition. As a result, the court overturned the full $1.55 million judgment that had originally been awarded to the sellers. The ruling explains the legal protections available to home buyers under standard inspection clauses in Michigan real estate contracts. By overturning the lower court's decision, the appeals court confirmed that buyers who honestly negotiate for repairs or a lower price based on inspection findings do not automatically lose their contractual rights or become liable for financial penalties.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘Diabolical regime’: Ex-US general warns Iran rebuilding nuclear programme
articles.summary: Iran is accelerating efforts to rebuild its nuclear and ballistic missile programmes despite US and Israeli strikes on its facilities, with satellite
articles.body: Iran is accelerating efforts to rebuild its nuclear and ballistic missile programmes despite US and Israeli strikes on its facilities, with satellite imagery showing construction and fortification work at sensitive sites as Tehran prepares for the possibility of renewed fighting.Retired US four-star General Jack Keane said Iran had not abandoned its nuclear ambitions, arguing that the regime remained committed to restoring its capabilities despite ongoing diplomatic efforts to prevent a fresh escalation.“They certainly haven’t given up on it. It defines their regime,” Keane told Fox News, describing Iran as a “diabolical regime”. He said Tehran had recommitted itself to recovering its nuclear programme and accelerating its ballistic missile development after recognising the threat its weapons posed to its adversaries, according to the New York Post.Satellite imagery has documented activity at several facilities, including the Pickaxe Mountain complex near the Natanz nuclear site. The underground facility is believed to be buried more than 300 feet below the surface, making it a particularly sensitive target amid concerns over Iran’s nuclear infrastructure.According to The Wall Street Journal, Iran has also been reinforcing protection around nuclear facilities and security-related bunkers. Satellite images analysed by the Institute for Science and International Security showed that Tehran had constructed makeshift earth mounds around the Pickaxe Mountain and Natanz sites to complicate potential ground raids.The rebuilding efforts extend beyond nuclear infrastructure. Iran has used the pause in direct fighting to restore missile and drone facilities and replenish its arsenal, while strengthening defences against possible renewed US attacks.The developments come amid continuing uncertainty over Iran’s nuclear activities and international monitoring. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has called for urgent action to address its lack of access to Iranian nuclear facilities and insufficient information about nuclear material at the sites.In its latest quarterly report, the UN nuclear watchdog said the absence of access and information raised proliferation concerns, particularly regarding the Isfahan facility, which has been targeted in US and Israeli strikes.IAEA director general Rafael Grossi called for the longstanding disputes to be resolved through a durable, verifiable diplomatic agreement. articles.title: Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure a war crime: UN
articles.summary: UN commission notes Russian weaponisation of cold in nearly five years of attacks on heating plants and power lines.
articles.body:
Russia’s persistent attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure constitute war crimes as they weaponise the cold of winter, a United Nations commission has said.

The Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine laid out in a report submitted to the UN General Assembly on Monday years of Russian attacks on heating plants, power lines, gas facilities and other infrastructure since the autumn of 2022.

The report was issued as Russia has stepped up its attacks on such civilian targets. Moscow has sought every year since its full-scale invasion in February 2022 to inflict suffering on Ukrainian citizens with an apparent ambition of draining the country’s will and ability to continue to defend its territory.

The commission said it has investigated the impact on civilians of large-scale attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and their cumulative effect since 2022.

“The frequency, intensity and geographic range of systematic waves of attacks with hundreds of drones and missiles at a time have increased over the years and inflicted significant damage to Ukraine’s energy sector,” the report noted.

In particular, the report focused on the Russian attacks during the severe winter of 2025–2026, when temperatures dropped to minus 21 degrees Celsius (-5.8 degrees Fahrenheit). That left millions of people in Ukraine facing lengthy outages of heating, electricity, water and gas, and forced them to cope with intolerable living conditions, it said.

The commission assessed that the Russian commanders ordering the attacks knew that the heating facilities they targeted were indispensable to the civilian population.

“Russian authorities have made official declarations concerning further attacks and referred to a plan to carry them out. The commission concluded that they committed war crimes of intentionally directing attacks against civilian objects,” the report concluded.

Erik Mose, chair of the commission, noted that as the cold season approaches, “the attacks have intensified once again, raising serious concerns about the threats to civilians’ lives and health”.

Russia and Ukraine have continued their daily attacks on one another as winter approaches, with little indication that a ceasefire might be in sight.

On Monday, a Russian strike on Ukraine’s southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia injured four people overnight, regional governor Mykhailo Semikin said on Telegram.

The Ministry of Defence in Moscow accused Ukraine of repeatedly striking the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine ahead of a planned local ceasefire this week.

The UN commission, which was set up by the Human Rights Council, in its report also accused Moscow of human trafficking in connection with the recruitment of foreign fighters into the Russian armed forces “in violation of international human rights law”.

“The majority of those recruited have been killed, went missing, while others have also been injured or captured,” the report read.

For instance, there have been numerous reports during the nearly five-year war of men from India having been duped into fighting on the front lines .

articles.title: An Arizona father repeatedly travelled to Michigan to see his child under a custody order, but the mother obtained a protection order accusing him of harassment; an October 23 appeals court ordered that protection order cancelled
articles.summary: A father who repeatedly travelled from Arizona to Michigan to see his child under a court-ordered custody agreement has won an appeal to clear his name.
articles.body: A father who repeatedly travelled from Arizona to Michigan to see his child under a court-ordered custody agreement has won an appeal to clear his name. The decision came after a court cancelled a protection order that the child's mother had obtained against him. In a ruling issued on October 23, 2026, the Michigan Court of Appeals overturned a lower court decision that had kept an emergency personal protection order in place against the father. The appeals court directed the Wayne Circuit Court to issue a formal order ending the protection order. The ruling ends a long-running legal dispute over court authority and the enforcement of custody rights between the parents. Court documents published by Justia Law identify the parents as TB and LRW.Arizona granted custody enforcementThe dispute began after the couple separated and the mother moved with their minor child from Arizona to Michigan. The father continued to live in Arizona and turned to the courts to establish and protect his parental rights. In October 2023, the Michigan Court of Appeals ruled that Arizona had legal authority over the child's custody case under the Uniform Child-Custody Jurisdiction and Enforcement Act. Following that decision, an Arizona court granted the parents joint legal custody in December 2024. In its custody ruling, the Arizona court found that the mother had deliberately kept the father away from the child by preventing scheduled visits. To address the problem, the court ordered the father to collect the child directly from the mother's home in Michigan for his first period of parenting time. The father repeatedly travelled to Michigan after giving advance notice that he intended to collect his child. However, the mother refused to carry out the scheduled exchanges. The father could not find the child in the state, so he began legal proceedings to enforce the custody order in Michigan's Oakland Circuit Court in January 2025.Protection orders sought during litigationSoon after the father filed his enforcement case, the mother asked the Wayne Circuit Court for an emergency personal protection order without first notifying him. She accused him of stalking and harassment. The court granted the order on January 31, 2025. The father later stated in court filings that he had never been properly served with the order. He said he only learned that it existed several months later, when he received a notification from the Michigan State Police. During the same period, the mother also applied for similar protection orders in Arizona. Judges in Arizona dismissed her requests after hearings, finding that she had not provided enough evidence to support her claims. One Arizona judicial officer noted that the evidence strongly suggested the mother was using protection orders to get around court-ordered parenting time and prevent the custody order from being enforced. Despite these decisions, the Wayne Circuit Court rejected the father's request to end the Michigan protection order at a hearing in July 2025. The trial judge relied heavily on the mother's testimony and declined to review documents about the ongoing custody decisions made by courts in Arizona and Michigan.Appeals panel finds trial court erredAfter reviewing the case, the Michigan Court of Appeals found that the trial court had made serious errors when issuing and keeping the emergency protection order in place. The appeals court explained that an emergency protection order requires specific evidence showing that immediate and lasting harm could occur if the other party were notified before the order was issued. The court found that the mother's application did not provide the necessary facts and failed to meet this legal requirement. The appeals court also ruled that the trial judge had wrongly ignored important evidence about the father's lawful efforts to enforce his parenting rights. Under Michigan law, trying to contact one's child or going to a residence with police officers to carry out a valid court order does not, by itself, amount to unlawful harassment. Although the protection order was due to expire in early 2026, the appeals court stressed that the legal challenge was still important. Keeping an invalid protection order in state law enforcement databases can leave a lasting record that damages a person's reputation and limits certain legal rights, including the ability to obtain a firearm licence. The Michigan Court of Appeals directed the lower court to issue an immediate order formally ending the protection order when the case returns to the circuit court.You use AI every day. articles.title: Britain sanctions Sudanese commanders over weaponised rape
articles.summary: Commanders from the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and Sudanese Armed Forces face travel and asset freezes.
articles.body:
The United Kingdom has sanctioned 15 Sudanese military commanders, militia leaders and security officials from both sides of the ongoing civil war accused of committing war crimes during the fall of the city of el-Fasher.

Commanders from the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces were sanctioned for sexual violence, torture and attacks on civilians. The measures include travel bans and asset freezes, with the wider aim of ensuring that “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”, the UK Foreign Office said.

The announcement came after the release of UK-funded reporting by the Centre for Information Resilience, which revealed a campaign of “systematic starvation and conflict-related sexual violence against civilians in Sudan”, the Foreign Office added.

On Monday, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said those who perpetrated crimes against humanity “must be held accountable and support from all external backers to the warring parties must end”.

The move comes one year after the fall of the city of el-Fasher, which became a focal point of Sudan’s war last year as civilians faced a prolonged siege, reported mass killings, widespread sexual violence and attacks on hospitals.

According to Miliband, “The war in Sudan has created a humanitarian catastrophe.”

“A year on from the atrocities in El Fasher, UK-funded investigations have shown that rape and starvation are still being weaponised against the people of Sudan,” he said.

Sanctions were announced against Hussein Abu Jalak, an RSF colonel linked to atrocities during the siege of el-Fasher, and Al-Nour Ahmed Adam, also known as “al-Qubba”, who was identified as present and playing a prominent role in besieging and attacking the city, the Foreign Office added in the statement.

It added that the UK has allocated five million pounds ($6.6m) to support survivors of sexual violence in Sudan and another 10 million pounds ($13.3m) in humanitarian aid.

Tens of thousands of civilians have been killed and 14 million people displaced since the war broke out in April 2023, according to Amnesty International.

articles.title: Angel mom confronts Indian illegal immigrant truck driver who killed her son, his wife in Oregon crash
articles.summary: An emotional video captures Erika Kirk-like compassion as a grieving mother speaks to Rajinder Kumar, the truck driver facing manslaughter in Oregon.
articles.body: An emotional video shows a grieving mother delivering compassion to her son's alleged killer. Video from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's Victims of Immigrant Crime Engagement (VOICE) office showed Elizabeth Carter, the mother of William Carter, speaking to the Indian illegal immigrant semi-truck driver charged with killing her son and his newlywed wife. The couple perished in an Oregon highway crash in November 2025. "Hello Mr. Kumar, my name is Elizabeth Carter; I'm William Micah Carter's mother," she told Rajinder Kumar, 32, fighting back tears and emotion as he appeared to struggle to meet her gaze. "And I wanted you to know that I pray for you and your family, I know you didn't get up that morning planning to kill two newlyweds. And I know your family is going through something important too." ANGEL MOM PLEADS WITH HER PARTY TO 'GROW UP' ON IMMIGRATION AFTER NEWLYWED SON KILLED IN TRUCK CRASH The interaction took place at the passenger window of an ICE vehicle earlier this month as federal agents prepared to transfer Kumar back to Oregon state custody to face criminal prosecution. Kumar faces two counts of first-degree manslaughter and three counts of recklessly endangering another person in Deschutes County stemming from the fatal wreck. Kumar is accused of killing William Micah Carter, 25, and his wife, Jennifer Lynn Lower, 24, who had been married for just 16 days. The deadly collision occurred on Nov. 24, 2025, when Kumar allegedly jackknifed his commercial tractor-trailer across U.S. Highway 20, blocking both lanes of traffic. The couple’s Subaru Outback struck the semi, killing both passengers at the scene. WATCH: 'LIFELONG DEMOCRAT' ADMITS SHE IS ‘ASHAMED’ OF PARTY AFTER SON KILLED IN ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CRASH Kumar was subsequently indicted by a Deschutes County grand jury. While he pleaded not guilty in state court, a jurisdictional battle erupted between federal and local authorities following his release. Court and immigration records show that Kumar entered the United States unlawfully near Lukeville, Ariz., on Nov. 28, 2022, when he was apprehended by U.S. Border Patrol and subsequently released into the country under the Biden administration pending removal proceedings. During that period, he was granted federal work authorization and later obtained a commercial driver's license (CDL) issued by the State of California. DOJ SUES CONNECTICUT, NEW HAVEN OVER SANCTUARY POLICIES: 'OPEN DEFIANCE' Following Kumar’s indictment in Oregon, ICE lodged an immigration detainer requesting that Deschutes County Jail notify federal agents before releasing him. County corrections officials declined to honor the federal detainer on April 2 and released Kumar into the community under Oregon’s state sanctuary policies. ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) Seattle agents tracked down and arrested Kumar in connection with his immigration case on April 22, detaining him at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, Wash., while moving forward with federal removal proceedings. EXCLUSIVE: DHS HONORS ANGEL FAMILIES DURING NATIONAL CRIME VICTIMS WEEK, CALLS CRIMES 'COMPLETELY PREVENTABLE' ICE ERO Seattle announced it has returned Kumar to Deschutes County authorities to ensure he faces a local trial on the felony manslaughter charges before any deportation orders are executed. "Two Americans lost their lives, and their families deserve accountability," ICE ERO Seattle acting Field Office Director Julio Hernandez said. "ICE worked closely with law enforcement partners to ensure Kumar is returned to state custody to answer for the serious charges against him. "This coordinated action protects the public, supports the victims' families, and ensures that an individual accused of these crimes does not evade justice." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Department of Homeland Security officials confirmed that federal deportation proceedings remain paused while Oregon state prosecutors pursue the criminal charges against Kumar, with criminal trial proceedings pending in Deschutes County Circuit Court.

articles.title: Coronation Street's Ian Puleston-Davies returns to soap after 11 years
articles.summary: The Welsh actor is back as Owen Armstrong and looking forward to a "cracking" storyline.
articles.body:
Coronation Street star Ian Puleston-Davies is returning to the soap opera more than a decade after he left.

The 67-year-old will reprise his role as Owen Armstrong almost 11 years after the character left Weatherfield, following the collapse of his business and breakdown of his relationship with Anna Windass.

The no-nonsense builder's return will see him move in with daughter Izzy and grandson Jake, and making it clear he blames Anna Windass' son, Gary Windass, for his family's misfortune.

Puleston-Davies, from Flint, in Flintshire, said: "I can't wait to pick up where I left off 10 years ago.

"It's brilliant to be back and to get stuck into a cracking storyline. Owen's back and he's still angry."

Puleston-Davies will start filming Owen's return next week and will be back on screen on the cobbles in January.

Since leaving Coronation Street, Puleston-Davies has starred in dramas Pennyworth, Tin Star and After The Flood.

Coronation Street producer Kate Brooks said she was "thrilled" Puleston-Davies was back.

"He wreaks havoc on the street, and his relationship with Gary is severely put to the test," she said.

articles.title: United Airlines delays 150 passengers overnight following serious in-flight threat
articles.summary: United Flight 1681 made a swift U-turn back to Las Vegas after the crew flagged a potential security concern, triggering an overnight crew timeout, the airline confirmed.
articles.body: A disruptive passenger forced a Newark-bound United Airlines flight to make a swift U-turn back to Las Vegas late Saturday night, grounding the cross-country trip until Sunday morning. United Flight 1681 had just departed Harry Reid International Airport when the crew flagged "a potential security concern" in the cabin. The Boeing 737, carrying 150 passengers and six crew members, safely touched back down in Vegas at roughly 11:05 p.m. without any reported injuries, several news outlets reported. TRAVEL NIGHTMARE UNFOLDS AS MAJOR AIRLINE SCRAPS FLIGHT AFTER HARROWING 12-HOUR DELAY "United flight 1681 from Las Vegas to Newark on Saturday, Oct. 24, safely returned to Las Vegas to address a potential security concern," United Airlines said in a shared statement with Fox News Digital. "The flight was delayed overnight due to crew timeout, and departed for Newark this morning," the statement continued. While the midair scare was resolved without physical harm, the diversion triggered an overnight delay after the flight crew timed out of their legally permitted working hours. Fox News Digital reached out to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) for comment. In an air traffic control audio recording that ATC.com obtained, a controller can be heard asking pilots if a passenger in question was "compliant or restrained." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "The passenger does not know anything is going on," a pilot said. "The flight attendant saw him texting that he was going to hijack the aircraft and called me and we went lockdown. … No restraint, passenger is compliant because he’s unaware." The aircraft eventually departed for Newark Liberty International Airport the following morning. The FAA confirmed it is launching an investigation into the incident, while airport officials deferred further details to United Airlines and the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department, Fox 5 Las Vegas reported. The Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department confirmed that officials arrested a 25-year-old man on suspicion of making threats or conveying false information concerning acts of terrorism in a statement to People. He was subsequently booked at the Clark County Detention Center, according to the outlet. Fox News Digital reached out to the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department for additional details. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES The pilot informed Air Traffic Control the aircraft was still "grossly overweight" and needed to burn excess fuel before touching down, the audio recording shows. An overweight landing risks adding stress to the plane's landing gear and structural parts, per SKYbrary Aviation Safety. To avoid potential damage during an unplanned landing, planes will sometimes dump fuel or fly longer to burn it off. Reflecting this, flight paths show the aircraft made two loops to burn fuel before returning to land at LAS, per FlightAware. articles.title: US-Canada tariff deal 'very close', says White House adviser ahead of midterms
articles.summary: The United States and Canada are moving closer to a trade agreement as tariff negotiations between the two countries gather momentum, White House economic
articles.body: The United States and Canada are moving closer to a trade agreement as tariff negotiations between the two countries gather momentum, White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett has said, with the issue carrying political significance ahead of the November 3 US midterm elections.“The negotiations have picked up; they’re gathering steam,” Hassett, director of the White House National Economic Council, said during an appearance on Fox News’ The Sunday Briefing.He added that a deal was “very close” and that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had been speaking with his Canadian counterparts throughout the week.US President Donald Trump also expressed hope about the negotiations, telling Detroit’s Fox 2 that an agreement could be reached within a couple of months, potentially before the midterm elections.“We’re getting close to a deal, and a deal could happen that’s going to be very good for everybody,” Trump said.According to the New York Post, Trump indicated that while an agreement could come before the election, the timeline would depend on whether the terms were favourable to the United States.“I want to make the right deal,” Trump said, adding that he was focused on the long term rather than securing a quick agreement.The negotiations come after trade talks between Washington and Ottawa broke down in August, prompting both countries to impose retaliatory measures. The dispute has affected businesses and consumers on both sides of the border and emerged as a political issue in key battleground states ahead of the November 3 elections.Hassett attributed the earlier difficulties to political developments in Canada, saying the recent Canadian election and tensions involving Alberta had made negotiations particularly difficult.Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said last week that he had spoken with Trump about trade and remained willing to negotiate, but stressed that any agreement must serve Canada's interests.Carney is “ready to sit down and negotiate when the US is”, according to his remarks, while insisting that Ottawa would seek “a deal that’s in the interests of Canadians”.Canada's minister responsible for US trade negotiations, Dominic LeBlanc, has also been in discussions with Lutnick in recent weeks. A US official told Bloomberg on Sunday that the talks were continuing, although the prospects for an agreement remained uncertain because Washington believed Canada had not yet offered enough.The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive negotiations, said Trump would approve only an agreement that benefited the United States.Trump eases tariffs on some Canadian productsThe White House has recently moved to ease tariffs on selected Canadian goods, including following lobbying by Republican Senator Susan Collins of Maine.Collins said on Friday that the administration would remove 50% tariffs on Canadian plywood, bleached paper, cartons and specialised agricultural machinery, with the changes expected to benefit Maine's rural and coastal economies.Trump had also exempted road salt and other Canadian products from tariffs last month after a request from Collins. At the same time, his administration added duties on certain other goods.The moves come as Collins faces a competitive re-election contest in Maine, where the economic effects of the trade dispute have become a campaign issue. Her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, criticised the senator for seeking credit for tariff relief, arguing that she had acted because her seat was at risk.Hassett defended the administration's approach, saying Trump had prioritised Maine's interests.“President Trump has put the citizens of Maine first,” he said.The tariff dispute has also become politically significant in Michigan, another battleground state where Republicans face pressure ahead of the midterms. Trump campaigned in the state on Sunday, highlighting the possibility of a trade agreement with Canada.White House highlights fisheries as priorityHassett also offered a glimpse into the administration's economic priorities, saying support for fisheries in Maine and Alaska had received particular attention.“Almost above everything else that we've done at the National Economic Council has been working on Maine and Alaska fisheries,” he said, referring to European regulations that had affected exports of Maine lobster.Hassett said Trump had negotiated a temporary arrangement with European countries that allowed Maine fishermen to continue shipping their products to Europe.The administration has also stepped up its focus on the seafood industry. The US Department of Agriculture established its first Office of Seafood in April, while the White House unveiled an “America First Seafood Strategy” on Friday.The developments highlight how trade policy has become intertwined with domestic political concerns as the administration seeks to support industries and businesses in states crucial to the midterm elections.For now, however, the US-Canada negotiations remain unresolved. articles.title: Keir Starmer's government discussed moving out of 10 Downing Street
articles.summary: The building has been described as a "gloomy, mice-infested, bomb-curtained rabbit warren".
articles.body:
Sir Keir Starmer's government discussed moving out of Downing Street because of concerns about its suitability as a workplace, senior figures from his administration have said.

Ministers and officials from successive governments have privately complained that Number 10's rabbit warren-like layout can lead to a lack of collaboration among those working there.

James Lyons, who served as Sir Keir's director of communications, said over the weekend that "moving out was something that was discussed" during his time in post.

Two other senior figures confirmed that discussions were had about moving staff into an open plan space in another government department.

One source said a space inside the Foreign Office building, a short distance from Downing Street, had been identified.

Both stressed that discussions did not go beyond an early phase and it's not known whether Sir Keir himself was consulted.

There's no suggestion that the prime minister would have stopped living in Downing Street if the plan had gone forward.

10 Downing Street is more than 300 years old and is an amalgamation of three houses, which comprises more than 100 rooms.

The building was given to Robert Walpole, widely regarded as the UK's first prime minister, by King George III in 1732.

Lord Walker, the boss of supermarket Iceland and a former adviser to Sir Keir, told the Financial Times on Friday that Number 10 was no longer "fit for purpose".

He said: "I think we should turn it into residences, or a museum. It's a national treasure. It's amazing. But it's ridiculous.

"It's just a Stuart-era building, not fit for purpose. It has tiny, tiny meeting rooms, all on different levels. There are hazards."

Lyons, who led Sir Keir's communications operation from October 2024 to September 2025, posted on LinkedIn that "Lord Walker is 100% right".

He added that staff were "deeply envious" of other departments and described Number 10 as a "gloomy, mice-infested, bomb-curtained rabbit warren".

Lyons added: "Moving out was something that was discussed when I was in 10 Downing Street."

One source said "there were chats at senior staff level about moving to an open plan office in FCDO" (Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office).

They said they didn't believe the idea went far, but said "the reason for discussion was serious" and added that the alternative plan was "about staff being open plan and able to collaborate".

Sir Keir became increasingly frustrated at Whitehall's ability to deliver change during his time as prime minister.

He was accused of picking a fight with civil servants when he said "too many people in Whitehall are comfortable in the tepid bath of managed decline".

Darren Jones, who served as Sir Keir's chief secretary, told MPs last week that he "tried to abolish the Cabinet Office three times but failed".

He proposed replacing it with a new department that would "abolish those barriers and walls and make them just one integrated team, focusing on the same things and really supporting each other to move it forward".

In his first days after succeeding Sir Keir, Andy Burnham created the Office for the Prime Minister and Cabinet.

The move was seen as an attempt to ensure that things happen when metaphorical levers of power are pulled.

It comprises Number 10, Number 10 North and other key parts of the Cabinet Office and is led by the UK's most senior civil servant, Dame Antonia Romeo.

The government says the new office will "ensure the centre of government is focused on our top strategic priorities".

Those around Burnham say he is yet to form a view about the adequacy of Number 10 as a workplace.

articles.title: Star Trek actor Walter Koenig, who played Pavel Chekov, dies aged 90
articles.summary: He played the eager Russian crewman in the original Star Trek series and later appeared in Babylon 5.
articles.body:
Walter Koenig, who played the spirited Russian crewman Pavel Chekov in the original Star Trek TV series, has died aged 90.

The US actor was a mainstay on the show as the eager and earnest navigator of the Starship Enterprise from season two in 1967 until it ended in 1969, later reprising his role in the six original cast movies from 1979 through to 1991.

In the mid-late 1990s, Koenig portrayed a very different character, the ruthless Psi Corps telepath Alfred Bester, in another sci-fi space series, Babylon 5.

His Star Trek co-star George Takei led the tributes on social media on Monday, writing: "Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend."

Koenig's Chekov added heart and humour to the adventures of the crew, led by William Shatner as Captain James T. Kirk.

Takei, who played Hikaru Sulu, added: "Rest well, my dear friend. Keep navigating a steady course."

Representatives for Koenig said in a statement given to the BBC: "Today we mourn the passing of Walter Koenig, whose talent, warmth, and unforgettable performances left a lasting mark on generations of fans around the world."

They confirmed he had died "of old age at home in North Hollywood" on Sunday night, "surrounded by his daughter and niece".

Born in Chicago and raised in Manhattan, Koenig was the son of Soviet Jewish immigrants whose family had lived in Lithuania.

He studied at the famous Neighborhood Playhouse School of the Theatre in New York, alongside the likes of James Caan, Christopher Lloyd and Dabney Coleman.

His big break came as the capable young Chekov, who would often joke that everything was invented in Russia.

The character was introduced to appeal to younger audiences, with his Beatles/Monkees-style mop-top haircut.

But Star Trek creator Gene Roddenberry's studio also publicised the role as a response to criticism in Pravda, the main newspaper of the Soviet Communist Party, about the lack of a Russian character. This was a claim Koenig later denied.

The American show, which aired during the Cold War and Space Race between the US and Soviet Union, imagined a future in which nations worked together to explore the galaxy, and Chekov's Russian heritage fitted that ideal.

Koenig once said that the character's purpose on the NBC show was to "set out the bones of the plot and let McCoy, Spock and Kirk fill it in", according to the Hollywood Reporter.

He was arguably more integral to the plot of the movies, being nominated by the Academy of Science Fiction, Fantasy & Horror for his work on The Wrath of Khan (1982) and The Voyage Home (1986).

His seventh Star Trek film appearance was a brief one in Generations (1994) - mainly a next generation film - and he later voiced President Anton Chekov in Star Trek: Picard in 2023.

He also wrote an episode for the original show's animated spin-off.

A published author, Koenig's other on-screen credits included Columbo and Futurama.

Earlier this year, his performance in the short film Mr Fleischmann saw him collect the Platinum Award for best actor at the 2026 Independent Shorts Awards, in recognition of his craft and career.

He married Judy Levitt, who appeared with him in three Star Trek movies and Michael Straczynski's futuristic space opera Babylon 5, in 1965. And they were together until her death in 2022.

The family suffered a personal tragedy in 2010, when their son Andrew, who played Richard "Boner" Stabone on the ABC sitcom Growing Pains, died by suicide aged 41.

Koenig is survived by their daughter, the actress and screenwriter Danielle Koenig, who worked on the animated series Star vs. the Forces of Evil.

articles.title: Machado finally made it back to Venezuela. Her challenge now is to pressure Rodríguez without upsetting the US
articles.summary: María Corina Machado’s return to Venezuela not only challenges Washington’s vision for the country’s transition, it also puts pressure on acting President Delcy Rodríguez by heightening tensions within her ruling party, which until this Sunday appeared to be weathering the aftershocks of Nicolás Maduro’s capture without major upheaval.
articles.body: María Corina Machado’s return to Venezuela not only challenges Washington’s vision for the country’s transition, it also puts pressure on acting President Delcy Rodríguez by heightening tensions within her ruling party, which until this Sunday appeared to be weathering the aftershocks of Nicolás Maduro’s capture without major upheaval. The opposition leader’s presence on the ground disrupts the relative calm which many have come to call the South American country’s “new political moment” following the US military operation that seized Maduro on January 3. In exchange for remaining in power, the Washington-backed Venezuelan government amended some laws, released dozens of political prisoners, allowed some exiles to return, and gave a company that partnered with the Pentagon privileged access to the South American country’s vast oil reserves. Machado’s unexpected appearance at the Santa Rosa church in Barquisimeto on Sunday, in west-central Venezuela, will also test the Rodríguez-US relationship, which appears to be much stronger than the connection the opposition leader currently has with the Donald Trump administration. “The relationship with Washington is strained but not broken. We are aware that the United States is our main strategic ally,” a source close to Machado told CNN. Machado must now push ahead with her political goals while balancing the delicate relationship with the US. Clash of interests Washington’s interest in designing an institutional framework for Venezuela without the upheaval that Machado’s presence and her demand for change cause within Chavismo — the socialist political movement named after former President Hugo Chávez — was already clashing with her need to establish herself in the country to regain political momentum, which had begun to fade after a period of just over two years, part of which she spent living underground in exile. The conflict between the interests of Washington and Machado became even more evident after the double earthquake on June 24. After that, Machado stepped up pressure to return to Venezuela, something the United States had advised against for security reasons. She tried several times, unsuccessfully, to return from Panama, where she had lived in recent weeks. She was never able to do so “because of the regime’s blockade,” Pedro Urruchurtu, director of international relations for the Vente Venezuela party, said in a statement published Sunday. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that any “impediments” to her return “had nothing to do with us.” He said that the only time he “personally” had discouraged her from returning to Venezuela was “right after the earthquake” because “the only thing we were focused on from a logistical standpoint was getting as many planes with relief aid as possible into the country.” She finally succeeded four months after the tragedy without Washington’s expressed approval. “We felt that it was not the time to ask, but to act. We preferred to act independently so as not to bother anyone,” a source close to Machado told CNN. “And, apparently, the United States did not object. We assume they must have found out beforehand because they know everything,” the source added. President Trump told CNN that he was unaware of Machado’s return but hoped she was well. Rubio said on September 1 that Washington had concerns about her possible return but that she did not need the United States’ approval. Rubio then said Sunday on X that “the conditions allowing for the safe return” of Machado were “the direct result of the US-backed reconciliation talks, which have already secured the release of hundreds of political prisoners and the return of hundreds of Venezuelan opposition figures.” “The United States expects the freedoms of all sectors of Venezuelan politics to continue to be respected, and we expect all political actors to support these talks,” Rubio added. With this, Washington appears to be setting the ground rules for Venezuela’s transition. It does not oppose Machado’s return, but it does expect that the pressure the Venezuelan leader will exert on Chavismo when she resumes her political activities will not jeopardize the negotiations between delegations from the Rodríguez government and a sector of the opposition, which will eventually culminate in presidential elections, as the acting president herself has acknowledged. Rodríguez on Monday declined to say whether Machado would be involved in the reconciliation talks but said she hopes the ongoing dialogue will offer a space for all “voices of good” to be heard. Without naming Machado, she also said she hopes that “those who have harmed Venezuela, those who called for sanctions and external aggression, feel some remorse and regret.” The Venezuelan government has in the past criticized Machado for urging the US to take action against the Maduro regime, including sanctions. Asked about whether Rodríguez can be trusted on a democratic transition, given some of her rhetoric around “external aggression,” Rubio said, “we ultimately judge it not by rhetoric but by action.” “If at the end of the day we have a new TSJ (Supreme Justice Tribunal), a new CNE (Electoral Council), a new election, and a new, you know, system of government, that’s what we want,” he said. The challenges ahead Machado’s team is aware that she is returning to a different country. There have been no major changes in the local economy, still weighed down by the loss of three-quarters of GDP and now seeking to recover from the effects of the double earthquake. “She has to get a feel for the streets again and see what the next steps are, thinking them through very carefully so as not to make a mistake. She understands that,” a source close to her inner circle said about Machado’s need to make direct contact with supporters in Venezuela after being in exile. The Vente Venezuela team, Machado’s political movement, has been preparing the ground for its leader’s arrival. Several of its senior figures, including two of the leaders who were confined to the Argentine Embassy compound in Caracas for more than a year, have returned to Venezuela to take part in rallies and events with party members, who are slowly beginning to resume their activities after the harsh repression that followed the disputed results of the July 28, 2024, presidential election. The opposition leader’s international relations team said in a statement that Machado is returning “to help build and promote a broad and pluralistic national agreement that will make it possible to develop a shared vision for the country.” “This agreement,” the statement adds, “must transcend political differences, foster understanding and reconciliation, and lay the foundations for a common future grounded in democracy, respect for human rights, peaceful coexistence, and prosperity.” For now, it is unclear whether Machado’s team is seeking to promote any agreement with the opposition delegation taking part in the US-sponsored dialogue. “That alliance would have to be built with her because it does not currently exist,” said a person familiar with the talks with the government. “But if we can establish coordination across the different fronts, it could provide major support for what is being discussed at the negotiating table,” the person acknowledged. Machado is not part of the negotiations being promoted by the United States, but she has said that she will not obstruct its efforts and will judge them by their results. Her arrival in Venezuela will energize a public that seemed resigned to waiting for the outcome of the US-backed talks, but she must be careful not to antagonize the country that, despite their differences, remains the key ally of her political project.

articles.title: Democrats, world leaders congratulate Trump critic Lula on reelection in Brazil
articles.summary: Democratic lawmakers in the U.S. and leaders around the world congratulated Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, commonly known as Lula, for winning an unprecedented fourth term Sunday. Lula, an outspoken critic of President Trump, defeated Flávio Bolsonaro in Sunday’s runoff election. Bolsonaro is the son of Brazil’s former far-right leader Jair Bolsonaro, who is…
articles.body:
Democratic lawmakers in the U.S. and leaders around the world congratulated Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, commonly known as Lula, for winning an unprecedented fourth term Sunday.

Lula, an outspoken critic of President Trump, defeated Flávio Bolsonaro in Sunday’s runoff election. Bolsonaro is the son of Brazil’s former far-right leader Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting a coup after he lost the 2022 presidential election to Lula.

Lawmakers in the U.S. more aligned with Lula’s brand of left-wing politics praised his victory and what it represents for the Western Hemisphere.

“Yesterday, Brazil showed the world that the will of the people is stronger than the authoritarians who try to suppress it. Congratulations President @LulaOficial and congratulations Brazil,” Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) wrote Monday on social platform X .

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D), who hosted Lula during a state visit last month, used the English translation of a Latin American protest slogan — made famous by Chilean left-wing composer Sergio Ortega Alvarado and the folk group Quilapayún — in congratulating the Brazilian leader.

“The people united will never be defeated! Congratulations, President Lula,” Mamdani wrote Sunday night on X .

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), who caucuses with Democrats, also praised Lula’s victory.

“Congratulations to Lula on his extraordinary reelection victory in the Brazilian presidential election,” the senator wrote Sunday on X . “Lula has stood up for Brazilian workers & democracy — and will continue to do so in the next four years.”

Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) attributed Lula’s election victory to “fighting back against extremism” and urged Trump to “respect the results and not undermine Brazil’s elections.”

The U.S. president has not publicly spoken about Lula’s victory, as he supported Bolsonaro’s father, who has been dubbed the “Trump of the tropics.”

Other Democrats also applauded the election results, with Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), the ranking member on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, writing on social media Monday that the people “in one of the world’s largest democracies” had spoken, and she encouraged “all to respect the electoral process.”

Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), the ranking member on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, also congratulated Lula’s win Monday and called on the Trump administration to “support” Brazil’s democratic process and “the will of the Brazilian people.”

Brazilians reelected Lula at a time when the right has seen gains across Latin America. One of the region’s few remaining left-wing leaders Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum congratulated Lula on his win.

“Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won,” she wrote Sunday on X .

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, in congratulating Lula, said on social media that the relationship between their countries “has flourished under our partnership.”

“Let’s seize this opportunity to make it even stronger, together — to create major new trade opportunities, protect the environment, and build greater prosperity for both our peoples,” he wrote Sunday on X.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote that she congratulated “my friend” Lula.

“Democracy and multilateralism have won in Brazil. Europe’s partnership with Brazil is thriving,” she wrote Monday on X . “We will remain by your side for the years to come. Together we will keep working closely for free and open trade. A rules-based global order. And strong ambitions for our climate.”

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi gave the Brazilian leader the “heartiest of congratulations to my dear friend” and called his victory “remarkable.”

“I look forward to working closely with him to further deepen and expand the multifaceted India-Brazil Strategic Partnership” Modi wrote on social media Monday.

“Together, we will continue to strengthen our cooperation across diverse sectors, advance the shared priorities of the Global South and work towards a more inclusive, equitable and sustainable world.”

articles.title: Colorado pro-life sidewalk counselor battles state 'bubble law' she says curtails First Amendment
articles.summary: Pro-life sidewalk counselor Wendy Faustin tells Fox News Digital that Colorado's "bubble law" could land her in jail for offering abortion alternatives.
articles.body: A Colorado woman who offers abortion alternatives outside clinics is battling a state law that prohibits her from approaching someone too closely, warning the rule has turned what she considers a compassionate conversation into a legal risk. Wendy Faustin, a pro-life sidewalk counselor challenging Colorado's so-called "bubble law," told Fox News Digital the restrictions prevent her from quietly offering women information about pregnancy resource centers, adoption agencies and other alternatives to abortion. "If you're within 100 feet of the entrance to an abortion clinic, I can't approach someone within 8 feet to give them any alternative information," Faustin said. Last July, a federal judge rejected her challenge to the Colorado law. Her case is currently on appeal at the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit. CHRISTIAN WOMAN PLEADS NOT GUILTY TO NEW 'ORWELLIAN' CHARGES FOR STANDING AND SILENT PRAYER Colorado state law and a Denver municipal ordinance prohibit individuals from knowingly approaching within eight feet of another person without their consent to distribute literature or engage in protest, education or counseling within 100 feet of a health care facility entrance, including abortion clinics. Violations are classified as a petty offense, which carries with it a fine or even a possible short jail sentence. The U.S. Supreme Court upheld Colorado's 1993 law in its 2000 decision in Hill v. Colorado, ruling that the restrictions did not violate the First Amendment. The restriction, she said, forces her to speak from a distance about an intensely personal subject, potentially allowing others to overhear conversations she would prefer to keep private. "I would rather be able to just walk up to somebody, offer them alternative information, places where they can get help," she said. PRO-LIFE GROUP SAYS MAIL-ORDER ABORTION PILLS VIOLATE FEDERAL LAW, URGES TRUMP ADMIN TO TAKE ACTION "I believe that every woman who is facing this decision deserves to have all the possible information that she might need," Faustin said. "Sometimes she's feeling kind of backed into a corner by circumstances or maybe by other people, and she may not be aware that there can be help somewhere for her through a crisis pregnancy center, an adoption agency, and so that's all the information that I give is offering her information where she can get help and also information about the development of her baby." Her attorney, Roger Byron, senior counsel for First Liberty Institute, argued the dispute extends far beyond abortion and raises fundamental questions about the First Amendment. DOJ WEIGHS CIVIL RIGHTS PROBE INTO FORT WORTH POLICE OVER ALLEGED FIRST AMENDMENT VIOLATIONS "These laws literally make it a crime for Wendy to approach within 8 feet of a woman," Byron told Fox News Digital, describing restrictions he says would not survive constitutional scrutiny if applied to other forms of protest. "These laws would be struck down immediately if they restricted anti-war protesters or union workers on strike outside of their employer's facility," Byron said. "However, because they restrict pro-life sidewalk counselors, they do not. This decision, Hill versus Colorado from the Supreme Court and the statutes that it protects, make sidewalk counselors, because of their pro-life message, second-class citizens. It literally creates two First Amendments. An oppressive one for pro-life sidewalk counselors, and the real one, the good one for everybody else." TRUMP DOJ EXPANDS RELIGIOUS LIBERTY PROTECTIONS AFTER MAJOR SUPREME COURT RULINGS "What's at stake is the free speech rights of anyone whose message is something other than what the government wants it to be," he said. Byron said the ruling at the Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit will determine what happens next. "I suspect either way, this case is going to end up in front of the U.S. Supreme Court," Byron said. articles.title: ‘New privacy law violates freedom of speech, threatens journalistic activity’: Digital news body may move SC
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Challenging the constitutional validity of various provisions of Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act and subsequent rules framed by
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Challenging the constitutional validity of various provisions of Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act and subsequent rules framed by govt, Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA) is likely to move Supreme Court, alleging that they were violative of the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression and threatened the full spectrum of journalistic activity.“It is prayed that sections 7, 17(2), 18, 19, 27, 29, 36, 37, 44(3) of DPDP Act and Rules 16, 17, and 23 of DPDP Rules framed under Section 40 be declared void to the extent they are in contravention of fundamental rights of the Constitution,” said the petition of the association, representing 21 of India’s leading media organisations.“The sections mentioned above fail to provide any exemption in favour of journalistic activity as a distinct class of processing, entitled to constitutional protection under Article 14 and 19(l)(a) of the Constitution and threaten the full spectrum of journalistic activity carried out by journalists, ground reporters, citizens, whistleblowers, RTI activists, and other stakeholders, and strikes at the core of our democratic framework and runs contrary to the basic tenets of the Constitution.”It said publishers, editors, reporters and correspondents will be brought within a regime of notice and prior consent, compelled erasure and verifiable consent, obligations that cannot be reconciled with the ordinary functioning of the press. Questioning the validity of Section 44(3) of the Act, which places every category of “personal information” beyond the reach of disclosure, without regard to whether it relates to a public activity, the petition said it dismantled the balancing mechanism between right to privacy and right to information that operated for two decades.“These provisions, taken collectively, constitute a disproportionate and excessive curtailment of the fundamental right to free speech and expression and the implicit right to know and access information as recognised under Article 19(l)(a). DPDP Act creates restrictions on the fundamental right to free speech and expression in relation to the dissemination of news,” the petition added.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: ESPN fumbles the Holy War by forcing Utah and BYU into a dreaded early-morning kickoff for fans
articles.summary: BYU and Utah fans face a 10 a.m. local kickoff for their rivalry game, and the Big 12 "Holy War" deserved a late night college football slot.
articles.body: The annual 'Holy War' between Utah and BYU deserves better. Once we get to this part of the season, television networks have to obviously start picking what they think are the most opportune times to broadcast some of the most important games they have under contract. But, that doesn’t mean companies need to sacrifice and give into the pressure of opposing conference games in order to get the better rating. And yes, I understand ESPN has the television rights to SEC and Big 12 football, so decisions like this are not easy for the programming department. LINCOLN RILEY'S TENURE SHOULD END WITH LOSS AGAINST OHIO STATE'S BACKUP QB, WITH A $70 MILLION BUYOUT Though, making Utah and BYU play at 10 a.m. local time feels criminal in this case, given the ramifications around this Big 12 game that has major CFP implications. If you haven’t seen the news yet, here is how ESPN decided what was best for the November 7th slate of games that are filled with must-see showdowns. MORE QUESTIONS THAN ANSWERS: ARCH MANNING LIKES THE DISRESPECT, BIG 12'S DISASTER AND A CFP RACE IN DISARRAY BYU vs. Utah: 12 p.m ET on ABC/ESPN Texas vs. Missouri: 12 p.m. ET on ABC/ESPN Alabama vs. LSU: 3:30 p.m. ET on ABC Kentucky vs. Tennessee: 6:15 p.m. ET on ESPN Georgia vs. Ole Miss: 7:30 p.m ET on ABC And, NBC will broadcast the Miami vs. Notre Dame showdown at 7:30 pm ET, while Oregon will face Ohio State at 3:30 p.m. ET on CBS. College football fans deserved a night-game showdown in Utah So, that left the important Big 12 game between the Cougars and Utes as the odd-teams out of this television equation that will see a plethora of top-25 showdowns take place on the same day. Look, I get that ESPN was put into a spot, but this could have easily been handled by the network putting the anticipated 'Holy War' in the 9:30 pm ET time slot after Kentucky faced-off with Tennessee on ESPN. It should also be noted that the Big 12 essentially gets the 3rd round pick on these weekends, and BYU just lost to UCF this past Saturday. But, make it a 10:00 p.m. ET kickoff on the network, which is essentially what took place this past weekend when Houston played Utah in Salt Lake City. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP We should be awarding the fans in college football with a better situation than having them walk into the stadium at 8-9 a.m local time for a highly-anticipated rivalry game with so much on the line. This almost feels criminal to make both fanbases wake up this early for a top-25 showdown with CFP ramifications. Cougars vs. Utes should’ve been played after the SEC slate For this, ESPN should have put this game in the late window, even if they were sacrificing some of the ratings that were undoubtably coming their way. Did the network honestly think a large portion of the college football base would not stay up for a late kickoff that came after Notre Dame played Miami, or Georgia faced Ole Miss in primetime? I also understand the conundrum ESPN was in regarding this kickoff time, but both Utah and BYU deserved better. This one is a loss, no matter how the networks come out of this I'd imagine those within the Big 12 office in Texas are fuming at this decision, and rightfully so.

articles.title: What Vucic’s defeat means for Serbia’s foreign policy
articles.summary: Those expecting Belgrade to tilt towards the West may need patience while the new government deals with domestic issues.
articles.body:
Serbia has reached a watershed moment following 14 years of authoritarian rule by Aleksandar Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS).

Sunday’s election delivered a historic victory for the opposition Student List, ending the political dominance that Vucic and the SNS had exercised/enforced for 14 years.

As Belgrade prepares for a turbulent transition and the upcoming presidential elections in December, international observers and regional neighbours have been asking whether Vucic’s departure will prompt a shift in Serbia’s foreign policy.

However, while international analysts often anticipate a quick foreign policy pivot toward the West whenever an authoritarian regime falls, experts warn that internal consolidation will take immediate priority and any transformation will be gradual.

SNS’s defeat has brought a mixture of cautious optimism and uncertainty across the Western Balkans. Serbia’s relations with Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Montenegro and Kosovo have often been frayed by Vucic’s nationalistic rhetoric.

Aleksandar Popov, director of the Centre for Regionalism in Novi Sad in Serbia, told Al Jazeera that a rapid reset in regional relations was unlikely.

“These questions will not be on the agenda immediately,” he said, referring to relations with Serbia’s neighbours.

The new authorities will first have to tackle domestic problems, he said, including dealing with a system that has “captured all democratic institutions”, as well as problems in the judiciary, prosecution service, police and media sector.

“Tidying up at home” will take priority before “solving problems with the neighbours”, Popov said, despite noting that the outgoing regime had done everything possible to undermine regional relations.

While relations with Croatia are “not frozen” neither are they “the way they should … be between neighbours”, being marked by frequent sharp words.

Amid recent mass protests in Serbia, Vucic accused Zagreb of organising a “colour revolution”.

In addition, “relations with Montenegro are disrupted and issues with Bosnia and Herzegovina remain unresolved,” he said.

Croatia is the thorniest case, Popov suggested, noting that relations deteriorated as the SNS clashed with Croatia’s ruling Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ), which stems from a similar nationalist-populist stable.

“Zagreb would fire a poisoned arrow at Serbia and that gave Belgrade an argument to retaliate,” he said, describing a system that “functioned on the production of internal and external enemies”.

Meanwhile, behind the public hostility, lay a quiet convergence on Bosnia and Herzegovina, he argued, with Belgrade backing Republika Srpska leader Milorad Dodik and Zagreb favouring a third entity.

He expressed hope that a new government in Serbia led by experts and civic leaders, would work towards stabilising the region and revive Serbia’s hopes of joining the European Union.

“The previous government sabotaged EU integration and the EU will not accept a country without good neighbourly relations. The new government’s task will be to repair those damaged ties,” Popov said.

Beyond the immediate neighbourhood, global powers are closely watching Belgrade.

Under Vucic, Serbia maintained a delicate balancing act, refusing to impose sanctions on Russia despite heavy pressure from the EU, while simultaneously allowing ammunition to flow indirectly to Ukraine.

Of all elements of Serbian public policy, foreign policy will transform the least under the forthcoming governmental changes, Vuk Vuksanovic, a lecturer in foreign policy at King’s College London, predicted to Al Jazeera.

“Many international and domestic structures that shape Serbian foreign policy will remain in place,” he said, adding that Moscow never fully trusted Vucic, but viewed him instead as “the devil they knew”.

Russian influence will take a blow, with the end of uncritical glorification of Moscow in Vucic-controlled tabloids and media and intelligence cooperation to be downgraded, he said, but the new government is unlikely to adopt a hawkish stance overnight.

Serbian interests can continue to be served by ties with Russia, he asserted. “The country still needs preferential gas prices, the Kosovo dispute remains unresolved and parts of the public remain disillusioned with the West.”

“The new Serbian government will not see value in joining EU sanctions or adopting a hawkish stance toward Moscow,” Vuksanovic continued.

“Regarding Ukraine, Serbia will maintain its policy of not recognising the annexation of Crimea and Donbas. However, there is a question mark over ammunition deliveries, as the opposition viewed Vucic’s weapons sales to Kyiv as a cynical ploy to buy Western tolerance for his domestic rule.”

Another critical dimension of Serbia’s external relations is its close relationship with Israel. Under Vucic, Serbia established a strong partnership with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, marked by arms trade and technology exchanges.

Bosko Jaksic, a foreign policy analyst, told Al Jazeera that while ties will not be severed, recent controversial agreements will face scrutiny.

“The new government has no reason to abandon cooperation with Israel, but it will certainly re-examine newly concluded contracts – primarily those concerning Serbian ammunition exports to Israel and Israeli surveillance equipment exports to Serbia,” Jaksic said.

The analyst also noted that Netanyahu’s government has lost another “authoritarian, nationalist ally” in Europe after Viktor Orban’s removal in Hungary earlier this year. However, Serbia’s future stance will also depend on political developments in Jerusalem.

“How Israel positions itself toward the new authorities in Belgrade depends largely on the outcome of Israel’s own elections,” Jaksic added.

Looking at the broader geopolitical alignment, he emphasised that Serbia’s foreign policy will inevitably undergo a review.

He suggested that “the policy of ‘sitting on multiple chairs,’ which brought Serbia more harm than good, will certainly be re-evaluated”, and that it is realistic to expect Belgrade to strengthen ties with the EU.

But as Serbia enters a new political era, the international community should expect a period of intense internal reform rather than sudden geopolitical realignments, all of the analysts agree.

articles.title: ED in SC: NewsClick received 86cr in ‘illicit foreign funding’
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: In its appeal before the Supreme Court in the NewsClick case, Enforcement Directorate (ED) has questioned the news portal’s ownership and
articles.body: NEW DELHI: In its appeal before the Supreme Court in the NewsClick case, Enforcement Directorate (ED) has questioned the news portal’s ownership and service arrangements with foreign entities. The agency has said the Peoples Dispatch website was initially owned and controlled by NewsClick, while the American Justice and Education Fund was paying NewsClick to upload material onto it. The enforcement agency has questioned the commercial justification for those payments.ED filed a fresh plea in SC in the case against NewsClick and its ‘ illicit foreign funding’ with details of NewsClick’s modus operandi, its receipt of nearly Rs 86 crore in foreign funds through arrangements ‘designed to make foreign contributions appear as legitimate business transactions’.According to ED, the issue was not simply that NewsClick had received foreign money. The issue was that foreign charitable contributions were deliberately presented as investments and commercial payments to circumvent Indian regulations governing foreign funding of news organisations. The agency has cited recovered emails, company documents, financial transactions, valuation reports, contracts and statements recorded during its investigation as evidence.Agency sources said NewsClick had received payments from US-based Justice and Education Fund (JEF) for articles, videos and other content uploaded onto Peoples Dispatch. “The service agreement was a device for regular foreign funding rather than a genuine commercial arrangement,” a senior official said.“An email dated Aug 21, 2017, from the portal’s former HR head Amit Chakraborty explicitly discussed changing NewsClick’s company documents to obtain foreign investment without permission from the ministry of information and broadcasting. The email stated: The purpose of the same is that we want foreign investment without the permission of the ministry of information,” according to the agency.Sources said ED had relied on statement of the portal’s Prashanth Radhakrishnan that JEF owned peoplesdispatch.org only from April 2021 and NewsClick owned it previously. It was NewsClick’s team that determined content quality and terms, supporting its contention that JEF’s payments were not ordinary arm’s length purchases.Sources said NewsClick is also being investigated for Tricontinental and other international funding connections, keeping in mind a Jan 2018 email discussing how Tricontinental could begin operations in India through a private limited company receiving US investment, rather than immediately seeking approval to receive foreign grants as a non-profit.“This has acquired wider relevance following recent Fox News reports concerning tech entrepreneur Neville Roy Singham, Tricontinental and their alleged links to international protest movements, including demonstrations in Paris,” an official said.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
